notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0530.tlg012.1st1K-gr: τράκτυον is obscure (perhaps a kind of groats or pastry, cf. Latin tracta); left untranslated. κοινότητες, the Methodist technical term, is rendered "commonalities" (also rendered "communities" elsewhere). The Hippocratic saying quoted in 2.1 is not identified. In 3.1 the phrase "ἢ τῶν ἐν τῷ σώματι τὸ μὲν ἔξωθεν ἁπλοῦν" seems to need repunctuation after σώματι; translated accordingly.

4.1: 'Κιανὸς, ὃς καὶ Προυσίας ἐκαλεῖτο' is taken as referring to Cius, the city later renamed Prusias; grammatically it could refer to Asclepiades himself. 'Σέξστος' read as Σέξτος (Sextus). 5.1: 'ἐγκαταλήψεων' read as καταλήψεων. 6.1: 'ὄρος' read as ὅρος; the sentence 'ἐρεῖ γὰρ αὐτῆς ὅσα μὴ δύναται, οὐ τὰ μὴ ὑπάρχοντα αὐτῇ ὁρίζει' is obscure and possibly corrupt; translated tentatively. 8.1: 'ὁ δὲ σημειωτικὸν' read as τὸ δὲ σημειωτικόν; 'δεῖ μὲν γὰρ' in the pharmacy sentence seems to need δεῖται and is translated so. 'παρέμπτωσις' is Erasistratus' term for the spilling of blood into the arteries.

In 10.1 'τὰ ὑπὸ τῆς ὀφθαλμοῖς' read as τὰ ὑπὸ τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς. The names of the parts of the ear (κυβοειδῆ, ξυστήρ, κογχίον) are obscure and rendered literally. 'λιχανός' (index finger) is traditionally derived from licking; the text only says 'from its use'. The Homeric quotation is Iliad 7.99. Παρέγχυμα (Erasistratean term) rendered 'outpouring'.

Line 10.1: 'the very middle of the λαγών (flank)' for the navel is odd; probably γαστήρ (belly) is meant, and the belly is translated. 'Thorax' here evidently means the whole trunk. The Homer quotation is Odyssey 10.161. 11.1: ληχηνεῖον is read as ληνός, 'winepress', the confluence of the sinuses (torcular Herophili), but the form is uncertain. 'Erasistratus... he thinks': the Greek αὐτῷ is ambiguous; it may mean 'it seems to be a parenchyma for it [the brain]'. τότε is read as τό τε, and σαρκώδεις as σαρκώδης. The object of δέξηται is missing, perhaps through a lacuna at the page mark; '[air]' is supplied. διαζῶσαν should grammatically be διαζῶσαν agreeing with nothing (expected διαζωννύον); the sense is clear.

In 11.1 'ἐῤῥώδους' is read as ὀρρώδους (watery/serous part). 'ὀβολιαία' (obelial, sagittal suture) and 'χαλκοειδῆ' (bronze-like, i.e. cuneiform bones, probably a corruption of χαλκιδοειδῆ) are rendered literally. The text says the fibula supports the talus; anatomically this is confused but translated as given. 'τότε τῆς κνήμης' read as τό τε τῆς κνήμης.

συνδεχής read as συνεχής (continuous). 'ἐφ᾿ ὧν δὲ καὶ ἀρχὴ παντὸς μέχρι τῆς διὰ τρίτης' is obscure and probably corrupt; rendered literally. In the pneumonia passage the construction (φασὶν ... ποιεῖ) is broken. 'Through wine and snow' (δι᾿ οἴνου καὶ χιόνος) is odd and may be corrupt (perhaps χόνδρου, groats). 'ὁ ἡμιτριταῖος γάρ' has an unmotivated γάρ. The cohesive pneuma assigned to the cardiac condition and to the whole body follows the text as given. In the list, 'abscess at the collarbones' (ἐν κατακλεῖσιν) may correspond to the later abscesses 'in concealment' (ἐν κατακαλύψει) under the diaphragm; one of the two readings may be corrupt. 'Either hellebore' (ἑκάτερος) refers to white and black hellebore. The verse quoted on Bellerophon is Homer, Iliad 6.201–2. 'Origin of the nerves' renders a clause that is grammatically awkward (ἀρχὴν εἶναι νεύρων) and may be corrupt. 'The sacred [remedy]' (ἱερά) is the purgative hiera. 'Balaustion' is the flower of the wild pomegranate. Bissinus, author of a bladder drug, is unidentified. ἐξόποροι ('pore-opening remedies') is an uncertain word, possibly corrupt. Line 1: 'keiriai' are bed-girths (webbing); 'πικρᾶς' presumably hiera picra or bitter aloes. Line 3: ἀποφρακτικῶν read as ἐκφρακτικῶν (deobstruent), as the definition requires; the list of 'urging' drugs is disordered and possibly corrupt (pairings unclear; 'ἐλατήριον ἅλας' doubtful); ἔρις read as ἶρις, πτυούσης as πιτυούσης (pityusa, a spurge), στογγύλον as στρογγύλον; λινόζωστις taken as mercury (Mercurialis).

Line 1: 'twelve kinds' are announced but the list does not tally neatly; 'eleven kinds' of external pharmacy likewise. 'πεπτικῶν/πεττικῶν' (digestives) is odd as a heading for chest and cough remedies; the text may be disturbed. 'σανδαράχη' is realgar/red arsenic sulphide; 'ἀρσενικόν' is orpiment. 'Κτησιφῶντος' read as a plaster named after Ctesiphon. Line 2: 'ῥοιάς' read with 'παρέλθῃ' as wasting away of the caruncle; uncertain. 'λιπαῖνον τὸ ὀστέον' (greases the bone) is obscure, perhaps corrupt. 'κτηδών' rendered 'fibrous layer'.

17.1: 'five differences' of skull fracture, but the list runs on into other head affections; the text lists five fracture types then continues. *Apechema* here vs *apochema* in 19.1 (both = counter-fracture). 19.1: 'χοινικίοις πρίοντες ταῖς διὰ τῆς περιστρεφομένης' is defective (a noun is missing); rendered conjecturally. 'σύμφυσις εἰς αὐτὸ τῶν περὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αἰγίλωψ' and 'κατ᾿ ἰδίαν βάλλοντες' (of hydatides) appear corrupt. 'σμίλῃ διαστέλλομεν τιλτοῖς ξυροῖς' is unclear. 16.1: in the hypochysis definition 'ἐν τῷ φαίνειν' is obscure. 'ὑδροκηλη' absent from the scrotal list in 18.1 (but present in 'after'). 'Myokephalon' explained via μυίας (fly), though the name suggests 'mouse'.

ῥυαδικοί normally denotes sufferers from *rhyas* (wasting of the lacrimal caruncle), which sits oddly in this genital/urinary context; sense uncertain. 'ὁ τύλος' ('the callus') may refer back to the foreskin operations. In the sarcocele passage the text 'δεῖ μόνην τὴν πρὸς δὲ τὴν...' is garbled; translated as the sense suggests. ἐπιβροχήσαντες in the enterocele passage is taken as ἐπιβροχίσαντες 'noosing', not the glossary's 'affusion'. In the passage on fractures with a wound, 'τοῖς σοῖς' is corrupt and the syntax of the whole clause is loose; rendered approximately. 'ἄμβη' is the Hippocratic reduction lever, left untranslated. 'πρὸς τὸν δεύτερον' in the head-dislocation sentence is obscure. The statement that four hip differences are 'incurable' contradicts usual doctrine; text may be faulty. In the hydrocele operation the text says κατὰ τὸ φλεβωδέστατον, 'at the most veined part'; surgery would expect the least veined, so the text may be faulty.

nodes.text: GALEN'S INTRODUCTION, OR THE PHYSICIAN.

[How medicine was discovered.] The Greeks attribute the discoveries of the arts either to the children of gods, or to certain people close to them, with whom the gods first shared each art. So in the same way they say that Asclepius first learned medicine from his father Apollo and passed it on to human beings, which is why he is held to have been its discoverer. Before Asclepius there was not yet any art of medicine among human beings, but the ancients had a certain experience of drugs and herbs, such as among the Greeks Chiron the centaur knew, and the heroes educated by him, and all that is attributed to Aristaeus, Melampus and Polyidus. Among the Egyptians too there was the use of herbs and the rest of pharmacy, as Homer also testifies when he says: "The Egyptian land, the grain-giving soil, bears very many drugs, many good ones mixed, and many baneful." And from the cutting open of corpses in embalming, many of the procedures of surgery too are thought to have been discovered by the first physicians. Some things, they say, were thought of from chance occurrence, such as couching those with cataract, from coming upon a goat which, having had a cataract, recovered its sight when a sharp rush stuck into its eye. And the giving of enemas, they say, was discovered from the ibis, which fills the skin around its neck, like the bag of an enema syringe, with sea water and Nile water, and injects it into itself from behind through its beak. Herodotus the historian also says that in ancient times the sick were set out at the crossroads, and those who had met with the same diseases would advise the remedies by whose use each had been cured, and that in this way the substance of medicine was gathered together from the experience of many. But this experience was irrational and not yet rational. Complete medicine, however, filled out in all its own parts, [they say] Asclepius alone discovered as something truly divine, and that the Asclepiads, receiving it from him in succession among human beings, handed it down to those who came after, above all Hippocrates, who surpassed everyone and was the first to bring complete medicine to light among the Greeks.

[What the starting points of medicine are.] The starting points of medicine, then, are three: one of discovery, one from the establishing of the art, and one of instruction. Of discovery in medicine, simply speaking, the most ancient starting point, and one without reason, is experience, as among the Egyptians and all barbarians. Of bringing it into the system of an art, as with the medicine of the Asclepiads, the starting point is reason and experience. Of instruction, as Athenaeus says, or of transmission, as some say, the starting point is the study of nature. And Hippocrates too said simply: "The starting point of reasoning in medicine is nature first." For the Dogmatists begin from inquiry into nature, since from what is according to nature they can know also what is contrary to nature, and without knowing what is according to nature it is not possible to understand what departs from it. And in treating, likewise, they need the study of nature, since from the natural power of the remedies applied they grasp their suitability to the affections. Those of the other sects, however, having rejected inquiry into nature, each begin from the things by which they acquired their habit of applying remedies: the Methodists from the indication of the commonalities, the Empiricists from observation based on experience. For just as for the Dogmatists the starting point of reasoning in medicine is nature, so for the Empiricists the starting point is experience, which holds very many times and always in the same way and alike. For from it history too begins, and in accordance with it the transition to the similar. For the Methodists the starting point is the observation of the similar in what is apparent, or the knowledge of apparent commonalities.

[How many sects there are in medicine and what characterises them.] There are three sects in medicine: the Rationalist, the Empiricist, the Methodist. The Rationalist is the one that offers an account of nature, examines the causes of diseases, uses inference from signs to discover the causes, and adopts treatment, by way of opposition, from what the causes suggest. For opposites are the cures of opposites. There are, then, four things that characterise the Rationalist sect: the study of nature, the study of causes, inference from signs, and fourth, the causes themselves suggesting the treatment. The Empiricist is the one that looks to the concurrences of symptoms that accompany one another in the sick, and has observed the treatment suitable to the symptoms, neither knowing the affection nor examining causes, but content with observation, through experience, of what is applied for the symptoms; and it uses also the history of those who have had experience before, and the transition to the similar, from what has been tried to what is untried, but similar in its apparent form. For whatever they themselves have tried through experience of the same things, over many cases and very many times, and holding always in the same way and alike, or have come upon by chance and noted as being always the same and alike, these they use with confidence, without busying themselves about their powers arising from their qualities. They have also trusted the most ancient [physicians], who recorded what they had observed through experience, which they call history. They use also the transition to the similar, passing over to things that have not yet come into their experience, whenever they appear similar in their ready visible form: as mallow, blite, beet and dock. And among cereals, as groats and rice, and *traktyon*. And again among tree fruits, as pear and quince. These things, then, characterise the Empiricist sect: looking to the concurrences of symptoms, and neither to the affection nor to causes; second, the observation, in the case of the concurrences, of what is fitting through experience; third, the history of those who have had experience before; fourth, the transition to the similar. The Methodist is the one that attends to commonalities and to the observation of the similar. For they reduce all particular affections to two general ones, the constricted and the flowing, which they call commonalities. They recognise these from the conditions arising in the body, apparent in either case and not hidden. Hence they have no need of inference from signs: for example, the constricted [is recognised] from the whole body's being condensed, its flux checked, and every visible excretion impeded; the flowing from the surface of the body's being loose and the perceptible excretions being increased in any part of the body whatever. So the two general affections indicate to them a twofold kind of treatment: to relax what is constricted, and to restrain what is flowing. When they are combined, [the physician must] address what is most pressing. They say that all commonalities are apparent; of these some are pathological, as the constricted and the flowing; some therapeutic, as relaxing and restraining; and some temporal: beginning, increase, peak, decline. The commonalities in surgery are concerned with the removal of what is foreign. What is foreign is of two kinds: either it is from outside, or it belongs to the things in the body. What is from outside is simple, but there are three kinds of what is in the body. What is from outside, such as a splinter, an arrow, and anything that is foreign, indicates complete removal. Of what is in the body, one is foreign in place, as cataract, dislocation and fracture, which indicate transfer or restoration to their proper place. Another is foreign in size, as all abscesses and the swellings about the scrotum, and pedunculated warts, growths and condylomata, which indicate in some cases the use of division alone, in others the complete removal of the excess. Another is foreign by deficiency, not as being in excess but as wanting, such as all mutilations, as of the lips and eyes, which is why some are called hare-eyed and hare-lipped. Likewise also fistulas, and all burrowing sinuses and cavities and ulcers and everything of this kind that, by reason of deficiency, requires and indicates being filled up. Besides the four commonalities in surgery there is also the so-called prophylactic kind, which is itself ranked as a commonality, in the case of poisons and arrow poisons and all venomous and biting creatures, winged, land-dwelling and aquatic. For the genus common to all of them is their being destructive, not falling under the constricted or the flowing, but being a genus distinct from these; hence their therapeutic commonality too is distinct from that one, and is called prophylactic. So the Methodist sect too is characterised, first, by observation of the similar in what is apparent, but not in what is hidden, as in the Rationalist sect; for by this it is also distinguished, since in that one too there is observation of the similar, but in what is hidden. Second, that from the similarity in what is apparent it reduces all particulars to universals: the affections, the remedies and the times. But they do not, like the Empiricists, attend only to what is apparent; for these stop at particulars and know nothing universal. Third, by taking the treatment from the indication of the commonalities, and neither having the causes suggest it, as the Rationalists do, nor being content with observation, in the case of the concurrences, of what is fitting through experience, as the Empiricists are.

[Who were the leaders of the three sects.] The leaders of the Rationalist sect were Hippocrates of Cos, who also became the founder of the sect and was the first to establish the Rationalist sect, and after him Diocles of Carystus, Praxagoras of Cos, Herophilus of Chalcedon, Erasistratus of Chios, Mnesitheus of Athens, and Asclepiades of Bithynia, from Cius, which was also called Prusias. The leader of the Empiricist sect was Philinus of Cos, the first to cut it off from the Rationalist sect, taking his starting points from Herophilus, whose pupil he also was. But wishing to make their sect ancient, so that it might be older than the Rationalist one, they say that Acron of Acragas began it. After Philinus came Serapion of Alexandria, then the two Apollonii, father and son, of Antioch. After them came Menodotus and Sextus, who also strengthened it thoroughly. The Methodist sect was begun by Themison of Laodicea in Syria, who was equipped for the discovery of the Methodist sect by Asclepiades the Rationalist. Thessalus of Tralles completed it. Those after them were Mnaseas, Dionysius, Proclus and Antipater; and Olympiacus of Miletus, Menemachus of Aphrodisias and Soranus of Ephesus disagreed over certain points within it. There were also some Episynthetics, such as Leonides of Alexandria, and Eclectics, such as Archigenes of Apamea in Syria.

[Whether medicine is a science or an art.] Some of the Rationalists, among whom is Erasistratus, supposed that medicine has one part that is scientific, such as the study of causes and the study of nature, and another that is conjectural, such as therapeutics and semiotics. The Methodists call it a science throughout. Both missed the truth, and the Methodists most of all. For science is knowledge that is fixed, firm and unalterable by reason. This is not found even among the philosophers, especially in the study of nature; much less, then, could it exist in medicine; indeed it does not come to human beings at all. Hence medicine may fittingly be called an art. For an art is a system of apprehensions and thoughts, exercised together in quality and quantity, tending towards some end useful to life. Since medicine too has apprehensions, human ones, and these sufficient in number to form a system of them, and moreover exercised together, that is, connected with one another and in harmony, not disjointed, it would most properly be called an art, since the definition of art fits it, and the apprehensions in it tend towards something useful to life. For it entered into life for the preserving and healing of human beings. There being a twofold distinction among arts, some always attain their proper end, such as carpentry, shipbuilding and house-building; others aim at their end as a target, but do not always attain it, only for the most part, and hence they are also called conjectural. Medicine would be one of these, like rhetoric, navigation and archery. There is also another distinction among the arts, itself twofold. Some have their being in the process of coming about, and after their activity ceases no product of theirs is shown, such as dancing, lyre-playing, wrestling and every musical art. Others, while they are active, have no visible work at all, but are as it were preparatory of something that is going to be, and when they have left off their activity, then their product appears, such as statue-making, painting, carpentry and the other arts whose works remain afterwards. Medicine would be one of these. For while it is treating, its end is not yet displayed, as it is continually opposing the diseases; but when it has completed its treatments, then it has rendered the person healthy.

[What medicine is.] The Rationalists used definitions, the Empiricists outlines; but to inquire about these befits philosophers alone. The ancient physicians simply defined or outlined medicine as follows. Medicine, according to Hippocrates, is addition and subtraction: addition of what is lacking, subtraction of what is in excess, in human bodies. For what some thought to be a definition of medicine is not a definition: not entirely freeing the sick from their diseases, blunting their violence, and not taking in hand those already overcome [by them]. For the definitions of the arts come not from what they cannot do, but from what they can do. For one would be stating what it cannot do, [and] does not define [it by] what does not belong to it. The more recent [physicians] defined it thus: medicine is a science preservative of health and removing diseases; not correctly. For it does not itself bring these about; rather, these are accomplished from what it does, and not always. Hence it does not consist of these, but of the things it always employs. These are addition and subtraction. So Hippocrates said that medicine is the very things it uses, which it employs both in the healthy, when it preserves their health, and in the sick, so that they may be freed from their diseases; so the things it always does are what constitute it, not what is accomplished by them. For the art is one thing and its end another. For what it aims at is something other than itself, and of course it does not always have this with it. Hence, so long as it does not attain it, it is not called its end, but its target; when it attains it, [it is called its] end. So too navigation and archery are not defined by their ends. For they do not always attain this, but [they are defined] by what they consist of and by what they work through in order to achieve their ends. Almost all those after Hippocrates think this definition is correct. Herophilus [holds] that medicine is the science of things healthy, diseased and neutral. For it has knowledge of these three: of healthy things, namely those that cause what is in a human being to be so disposed that, when they are well fitted to one another, health is constituted; of diseased things, those that dissolve the healthy harmony; and of neutral things, which are all the remedies applied in diseases and their material. For these, before they are taken up by the physician, are neutral, neither healthy nor diseased.

[How many parts of medicine there are.] The primary parts of medicine are the physiological, the aetiological or pathological, the hygienic, the semiotic and the therapeutic. Athenaeus puts the material part in place of the semiotic, which [material part] is within the therapeutic. For without the material part the therapeutic could not exist. Inference from signs is necessary for treatment too, but it is not itself treatment. For treatment is accomplished through material, and the material part contributes nothing else apart from treatment. But the semiotic is necessary even apart from treatment, for knowing which [conditions] are treatable and which untreatable, and for avoiding the latter, so that we may not fail by attempting impossibilities. Each of the five parts of medicine also has a subdivision. The physiological part of it, then, is the one in which we deal with the nature of the human being. It is divided into the account of the elements of which the human being is composed, the account of the generation and formation of the embryo, and thirdly the examination of the external parts of the body, when we dissect or study the bones. The aetiological, which is also the pathological, is the one in which we examine what is contrary to nature, investigate the causes of diseases, and inquire closely into the concurrences of symptoms and the states of the affections. For without these it is not possible to set treatment correctly against them. The hygienic part of medicine is divided into the preservation of health, the prevention of diseases, and recuperation from diseases. The semiotic is also divided into three: recognition of what is past, examination of what is concurrent, and foreknowledge of what is to come. The therapeutic likewise is itself divided into three: diet, surgery and pharmacy.

[Whether the division of medicine into the five parts is necessary.] The study of nature is necessary because it is not possible to know what is contrary to nature without first understanding what is according to nature. For diseases arise contrary to the nature of these things. The study of causes and of affections are also necessary: the one so that we may see the causes of the affections, which must be opposed, the other so that we may also recognise the affections themselves, as named by the ancients, and their states. Useful too is the recognition of the symptoms concurrent with the affections; for from their coming together, which the Empiricists call concurrence, the affections are given their specific form. But the Empiricists observed, in the concurrences, what was fitting for each set of symptoms; for the Methodists the affections indicate the treatment, as for the Rationalists the causes do. Yet the Rationalists examine no less both the affections and the concurrences. But they assign everything to the causes; and of causes some are antecedent, some containing, some cooperating, some joint causes, some preceding. Antecedent are those that begin first and, having acted, depart, such as chill, fatigue, overheating, indigestion. A containing cause is one whose presence means the disease is present, and whose removal resolves it, such as a splinter or an arrow. A joint cause is one able by itself to produce the affection, but producing it together with another too, such as a stone in the bladder and inflammation; for both are causes of retention of urine, and each can also by itself bring on the stoppage of the urine. A cooperating cause is part of a cause, unable by itself to bring about the affection but working together with another, as sexual excess cooperates towards arthritis and rowing towards the bringing up of blood. A preceding cause is one either produced or helped by the antecedent cause; for example, an excess of blood arises from abundance of food, and precedes the transfusion [of blood] described by Erasistratus, which is the containing cause of all diseases; and without the preceding cause it does not occur. The hygienic part is placed before the therapeutic not only as a part of medicine but also as finer than it. For it is much better not to let someone fall ill in the first place than to free him from disease. Just as for a helmsman it is preferable to make the crossing before running into a storm than to escape after being storm-tossed and endangered. Within the hygienic part, again, keeping someone in health differs from warding off diseases that are coming on. For the one is achieved through the customary diet, while the other already needs therapeutic remedies in order to forestall and dissolve beforehand a disease that is about to form. For whatever affections they cure once they have arisen, these they also prevent from forming before they arise. Likewise recuperation differs from these. For the person recuperating is no longer in a state contrary to nature, but not yet according to nature; rather, having just been freed from what is contrary to nature, he is on his way to what is according to nature; hence he needs a different regimen, neither therapeutic, for he is not ill, nor that used for the healthy, for he is not yet fully healthy. Hence the kinds and amounts of things used for the healthy cannot be employed for such people. The semiotic part of medicine is most necessary for treatment by diet. For we inquire closely into both the symptoms that have occurred before and those present in order to find the cause of the disease. It is also most necessary for foreknowing whether the disease will be fatal or survivable. Likewise, conditions treated by surgery and by drugs are not dealt with without inference from signs, and they likewise need prognostic inference from signs in order to know which of them are untreatable, and which are treatable but cause great harm, or kill if they are treated. The therapeutic part being divided into diet, pharmacy and surgery, diet is a regimen of remedies that disperse, add and aid concoction, used in all sick people, but having its chief authority in the feverish. Surgery is the portion of therapeutics that heals people by incisions, cauteries and the setting of bones. Pharmacy is a kind of treatment that cures both internal and external affections by drugs alone. For it needs a suitable diet, and sometimes also requires surgery, just as surgery and diet also make use of pharmacy. We must therefore begin from the beginning, from the study of nature, since no one could correctly preserve people in health, nor determine the causes in the sick, nor infer from signs, nor treat, without having examined from what elements the human being is composed and how diseases arise when these are altered contrary to their original nature.

[On the elements of which the human being is composed.] The human being, then, in agreement with the natural philosophers, according to Hippocrates, is composed of the primary elements of the cosmos, of fire, air, water and earth; not as though the human being were composed of these themselves, but of things analogous to them. And in dissolution he is resolved into these primary [elements], as Hippocrates himself said: 'And again, when the human being dies, each thing must go back to its own nature, the dry to the dry, the cold to the cold, the moist to the moist and the hot to the hot. Such also is the nature of animals and of all other things. All things come into being alike and end alike. For their nature is composed of the things mentioned, and ends, in the manner mentioned, in the same thing; from whatever each thing was composed, to that it also went back.' As Homer too said, 'But may you all become water and earth', indicating the dissolution into these. As from secondary [elements], close to human nature, they say the human being is composed of the four humours, blood, phlegm, and yellow and black bile, because in the first formation of the embryo the constitution of what is being born comes about from the seed and from the blood flowing in from the mother through the urachus. And in these were the four humours. Others say that the human being, once already born, is put together from three composite [elements], namely from the moist, the solid and the *pneumata* (breaths). Hippocrates calls them 'the containing', 'the contained' and 'the impelling'. The containing, then, are the solid things, bones, nerves, veins and arteries, from which the muscles, the flesh and the whole bulk of the body are woven, the compound structures both of the internal and of the external parts. The contained are the fluids carried in the vessels and dispersed through the whole body, which Hippocrates calls the four humours mentioned above. The impelling are the *pneumata*. According to the ancients there are two *pneumata*, the psychic and the physical. The Stoics also introduce a third, the 'holding' [*pneuma*], which they call *hexis* (cohesion). Erasistratus too, positing the triple weave of vessels, nerves, veins and arteries, as the principles and elements of the whole body, leaves out the fluids and the *pneumata*. For he says that the animal is governed by these two materials, by blood as nourishment and by *pneuma* as a cooperator in the natural activities. But he does not take them as principles. Yet many other kinds of bodily parts are found which are not composed of the triple weave, for instance the brain, the marrow and all the bones. The brain or the marrow he ventures to call a *parenchyma* (outpouring) of nourishment, like fat, and likewise the substance of the liver, spleen and lung. But the bones he could not call an outpouring of nourishment, nor [say that they are] woven from the three kinds of vessels mentioned above. According to Asclepiades the elements of the human being are breakable corpuscles and pores. According to Athenaeus the elements of the human being are not the four primary bodies, fire, air, water and earth, but their qualities, the hot, the cold, the dry and the moist, of which he posits two as efficient causes, the hot and the cold, and two as material, the dry and the moist; and he introduces a fifth, following the Stoics, the *pneuma* that pervades all things, by which all things are held together and governed. Hippocrates, then, proceeded through three, calling the elements of the human being the containing, the contained and the impelling, by which he encompassed all the elements of those after him, and the study of nature according to elements and the aetiology of what is contrary to nature. But those after him, I do not know how, dividing into three this divine and truly Asclepian medicine, which is one, and tearing apart its naturally united parts, some attributed both the constitution of what is according to nature and the cause of what is contrary to nature to the humours alone, like Praxagoras and Herophilus. Others, positing the solid bodies as the principal and elementary ones, take both what is naturally constituted to be from these and the causes of diseases from there, like Erasistratus and Asclepiades. And the followers of Athenaeus and Archigenes declared that natural things are both constituted and governed by the *pneuma* alone that pervades them, and that all diseases arise when this is primarily affected; hence they are also styled Pneumatists.

[Names of the external parts of the body.] Concerning the external parts or members of the body, and what their names are, Aristotle first undertook to teach and to write. The later physicians too thought it necessary to treat the same matters themselves, so that they need not point out each of the parts or members by laying a hand on it, but might have a sufficient indication of them from the name. The followers of Erasistratus were especially zealous in this, like Apollonius of Memphis and Xenophon before him. The Egyptian physicians, then, divide the whole body into four, head, arms, chest and legs, but the others [divide it] into more, subdividing the four mentioned into other parts of the whole, not as members of those. Of the head, then, the whole cavity may be called a part of the whole body. Of this, the members are: the front part above the eyebrows, bare of hair, from ear to ear, is called the forehead, and the hairy part above it the *bregma* (front of the crown). The parts on either side of this, above the ears, are the temples. The part beyond the *bregma*, in the middle of the head, is the crown, from which the growth of the hair also seems to begin, like a circle from its centre. The part after the crown that goes down at the back towards the tendons [of the neck] is the *inion* (nape). At the front, everything below the forehead is called the face, bounded by the ears, eyes, nose and mouth as far as the chin. It begins from the eyebrows; for where the forehead ends as it comes down from above, the eyebrows succeed, as its projecting and hairy limits. Where the forehead extends to the temples, at its limits, the ears are set. Of these, the spread-out parts are the 'wings', and the parts bent back from the front, curving over at their very tips, are the 'cube-shaped' [parts], under which the semicircle, rounded and rising to a point, is named the 'scraper', and the hollow under their point the 'little shell'. The round hole in the middle is the auditory passage, below which is the lobe, the fatty part hanging from the ear. The part lying above it is the antilobe. Under the eyebrows are the eyes, which are also called *ommata*, [meaning] the whole form with its members. Of these, the parts covering the inner structure of the coats are called eyelids, one upper and one lower, meeting each other frequently and at their edges, to take up the sight and to ward off things that strike the eyes violently, and closing exactly, as in sleep, to turn away the faculty of sight, so as to bring the person to rest. Of the eyelids, the parts next to the whole eyes, where they meet each other, are named *tarsoi* (rims), from which grow hairs called eyelashes (*blepharides*), which have taken their name from what they grow on. They exist to direct the visual *pneuma* or, as some say, the rays poured out from within, for seeing clearly. Certainly, when these fall out or are broken off, the animal can no longer see so well straight ahead or far off. The inner limits of the eye, where the eyelids join, are called corners, the large one towards the nose and the small one towards the ear. Between them is the white of the eye, in the middle of which is the iris, a circle varied in colours, which is why it was called iris, from its likeness to the rainbow (*iris*) in the sky. The very centre of this, again, is the pupil, through which seeing is accomplished. The nose is set between the eyes; its parts on either side are called nostrils (*myktēres* or *myxōtēres*), through which animals breathe and smell. Of the nostrils, the outer parts are the 'wings', and what divides them the 'column'. On either side of the nose, the hollows under the eyes are called properly the 'hollows', from which some people are called hollow-eyed. Through diseases these swell up, from indigestion or discomfort. The parts rising above these between nose and ears are named the cheeks (*mēla*), which in those of better colour and more liberal [nature] redden in shame. The jaws are the parts going down from these towards the chin and ending there in its point. The chin is all that is under the lip, in a rounded, elongated shape. The moustache is the part above the lip, under the nostrils, which Homer called *hypēnē*. The mouth is the part in the middle of the lips, formed and enclosed by them. For these seem as if grown together, then split apart to make the mouth, which is why they look as if just divided. What receives the head as far as the shoulders is as a whole called the neck. Its back parts are properly named the tendons. Under the neck, on either side, the shoulders rise, of which the topmost part is called the *akrōmion* (point of the shoulder), and the part from this to the front the collarbones; between these is the jugular hollow. From the shoulders the arms come, each attached to the side next to it. Of these, the part from the shoulder to the elbow is called the upper arm. The elbow is where the whole arm bends, the outer part of which is named the *korōnon* and the *olekranon*. The part after this is the forearm (*pēchys*), with which people also measure. Where the forearm ends and makes a joint with the hand, it is called the wrist, and what follows is the metacarpus. Then the knuckles, where the fingers begin. Of the fingers, the largest is called the *anticheir* (thumb), because, working together with the whole hand, it can do as much as it. The one after it is the *lichanos* (licking finger), having its name, it seems, from its use; next the middle finger, and after it the *paramesos* (ring finger), which is dedicated to physicians and has received its name from them. Last of all is the little finger, in that it is smaller than all. The part from the wrist, then, is called the hand. When it is turned upwards, the raised part by the thumb is called the *thenar*, and the part opposite it the *hypothenar*. The part under the bases of the fingers is the 'breast' of the hand. The part between all these is the hollow of the hand. From above, all that is under the neck, from the front down to the flanks, is called the thorax. Of this, the parts under the collarbones and the arms on both sides are the ribs, from which each side is also called *pleuron*, and the part between these the breast. And its very middle is the breastbone, down to the cartilage, under which is the mouth of the stomach; the place is also so called from the outside. From here the *epigastrion* (upper belly) rises. The parts below the mouth of the stomach on the outer surface are fittingly called *hypochondria*, since they lie straight under the cartilage, as it were after it. They are muscles spread out and laid upon the peritoneum, and covered on the outside by the skin. By the same name the internal viscera too are called *hypochondria*, since they too lie under the cartilages of the false ribs and as it were inside them. The middle parts on the outside, those properly called *hypochondria*: the part in front of the flanks that surrounds the hypochondrium is the *epigastrion* (upper belly), and the part on either side the *kenеōn* (soft of the flank). The very middle of the belly is the navel. The part under this is the *ētron* (lower belly). Then comes the pubic region, which is also called the *episeion*. Into this the thorax ends, and there the private parts of males are placed, and those of females at the parting of the thighs, so that they may be hidden by them. Of the male [part], then, the projecting part is the shaft. Its tip is the glans. The place where it is pierced for excretion is named from its use the urethra; the part covering the tip is the foreskin. The lower part of the shaft along its length is the seam. The part stretching as far as the anus is called the *tauros* (perineum). The *didymoi* (twins) are also named testicles, inside and outside. And the scrotum is what surrounds the *didymoi*. Of the female private part, for so the ancients named it, the cleft itself is called the *kteis* (comb). The parts surrounding the cleft are the *pterygōmata* (labia). The small piece of flesh growing out in the middle of these at the division is the *nymphē*, which, because it often protrudes a great deal, is judged to deserve excision among the Egyptians in the case of maidens. Common [to both sexes] is the mouth of the rectum issuing through the seat, which serves to hold back excretions whenever we wish; it is called the *daktylios* (ring) from its shape and the sphincter from its action. The part under the neck at the back has this arrangement and naming. The whole is called the back. From here the parts on either side are the shoulder blades, and the part between them the *metaphrenon* (upper back), under which the gullet lies on the inside. The very middle of the whole back from above down to the buttocks is the spine. The part of this directly under the *metaphrenon* Homer called the *aknēstis*, and to make it clear he added: 'at the *aknēstis*, the middle of the back'. For along the straight line of its length the back is in the middle, and it is the middle between the *metaphrenon* and the loins. Next then come the loins, which are also named *ixys*, where we gird ourselves. These end at the sacred bone. On either side of this are the hips, on which are the buttocks. Because the underlying bones are very large, fleshy bodies were laid beneath them there. Their swellings, from being rounded, are called *sphairōmata* (rounded parts). From here the body, which was united, becomes divided in two. For it is divided into two parts, which are called legs, the parting of which the ancients call the *dichala*. These as a whole, down to their ends, are called legs; of them, the parts coming straight from the hips are the thighs. Where after these the limbs meet those below and make a joint, it is called the knee. Its back is the *ignya* or *ankylē* (hollow of the knee). The parts from here downward, very large limbs, are the shins. Of these the front is the *antiknēmion* and the back the calf. The ends of the bones of the shin, projecting both to the inner side and to the outer, are called ankles. The parts from the ankles are properly called feet. From them people also devised another measure for themselves, taking the foot. Of the feet, the back is named the heel. The front from the ankles to the toes is called the *tarsos*. Of this, the inner part, where the feet face each other, toward the big toe, beginning from the inner ankle, is the *pedion*. The part directly under this, in the middle of the underside of the foot, is the hollow. The lowest part, on which we tread and on which we step, is the sole. The raised part of this toward the toes after the hollow is the 'breast' of the foot. Then the toes, equal in number to those of the hands, but not given the same names, because they do not perform the same uses either, except for names drawn from difference in size or from the order of position.

[Anatomy of the internal parts.] Anatomy is said by an extended use also of the account of the external parts and members of the body, which is a description in words of each, with their natural position, order and use, which it provides to the animal, and the proper name of each, which we have already gone through; but properly anatomy means the laying open of the internal parts with reasoning. For it is not their being shown to the eye that is anatomy, but gaining knowledge of each of them with reasoning, and learning their natural activities, how they are accomplished through them, and the communications that the viscera and the other parts of the body have with one another through the vessels. The brain, then, does not appear to be woven from any of the principal vessels mentioned before according to Erasistratus, which is why he thinks it is an outpouring (parenchyma) of nourishment. It is a simple body, and for this reason principal and most sovereign of the parts in us. Hence they also entrust the ruling part of the soul to it, like Plato and Hippocrates. It is enclosed by two membranes: one adjoining it and moulded to it, which is called the *choroeidēs* and is more full of veins; the other, lying upon this, is attached rather to the skull at certain places, and is more sinewy. From above, then, veins from the heart channel nourishment into it at the so-called *lēnos* (winepress), from the arteries at the base. From here nerves also begin to grow out of it, whence they distribute the psychic activities into the whole body. There are two kinds of nerves: one, the binding ones, which hold the bones together with one another; the other, the sensory and motor ones, which produce sensation in the body and send voluntary movement into the whole, and from which the muscles are generated. The channels of the eyes too grow out from the base of the brain, through which the visual *pneuma* is distributed to the eyes. From here also outgrowths are attached to the nostrils, through which we smell and through which the brain is cleansed. To the ears there are no outgrowths. But this membrane is pierced at the back and makes a worm-shaped outgrowth, through which they too are cleansed; and at its beginning is the so-called *kōnoeides* (cone-shaped body). From here also the spinal marrow begins. The brain has two ventricles; according to some, one, where the ruling part of the soul is seated. The bones of the skull too are enclosed above, under the skin, by the membrane called the pericranium, which grows out from the membranes through the sutures; this becomes the origin of the membrane lining the ribs, of the diaphragm, of the peritoneum and of every sinewy membrane. The eye is composed, according to Hippocrates, of two coats, which Hippocrates calls membranes, since they grow out from the membranes [of the brain]. According to the more recent [physicians], of three, and according to some of four. First, on the outside, is the horn-like coat, white elsewhere, but where it thins at the iris it shows through the colour beneath, according to which it appears black, or bluish-grey, or light-coloured; second is the grape-like coat, resembling a grape on the inside, pierced at the pupil. Third is the net-like coat, which enfolds and as it were receives at its tip the fourth coat introduced by some, which they also call the unseen one. For it is a membrane very small and very thin. But the first and second are solid membranes and thick coats; the third and fourth are very thin. Hence Hippocrates too knows only the first ones, saying: 'The eye has two membranes.' These membranes enclose three fluids: the watery, the glassy and the crystalline. Of the eyelids, the inner parts are fleshy and the middle parts cartilaginous; on the outside they are covered by skin. Because of the hardness of the cartilage in between, fat is laid under it as a kind of cushion, which, when it becomes excessive, produces the *hydatides* (watery swellings). The tongue is fleshy for the most part; but a twofold kind of nerves grows into it from the base of the brain: one of the so-called soft nerves, through which it transmits the sensation of taste to the ruling centre; the other of the hard ones, through which voluntary movement too is brought to it. At its root grows the epiglottis, which in swallowing runs up and lids the windpipe, so that nothing solid or liquid may fall into it. For the same reason the *antiades* (tonsils) also came to be, four in number, two plainly visible at the root of the tongue on either side, and two next to these further in. These are also called *paristhmia*, because the place beside which they lie resembles an isthmus, and especially when they are inflamed, since they greatly narrow this passage. Since the animal is governed by two materials, nourishment and *pneuma*, the ways and receptacles of *pneuma* are these: nostrils, mouth, windpipe, rough artery (trachea), lung. Nose and mouth are for breathing, and the uvula so that cold air may not fall all at once into the windpipe. The rough artery is its passage into the lung, which lies in the breast, through which all respiration takes place, as it expands in order to receive [air], and contracts in order to send it out. Hence in its action it resembles smiths' bellows, and in shape an ox's hoof. When the *pneuma* has been worked up in the lung, the most necessary part is carried into the left ventricle of the heart, and the useless part is breathed out through the same ways by which it was breathed in. The vessels of nourishment, those for reception, and the organs for working it up are these: mouth and teeth, gullet, stomach, jejunum and small intestines. Mouth and teeth are for grinding; the gullet for appetite and swallowing. It is stretched alongside the rough artery and extends as far as the diaphragm. Common [to the whole] for digestion is the belly. It begins about the middle of the cartilage, where it is called the mouth of the stomach, and passing under the liver, being sigma-shaped in its cavity, it inclines to the left with its other end, where the pylorus is, so that its nourishment may not slip through all at once. The jejunum and small intestine are for distribution; the jejunum has many coils and is held together by the *mesaraion*, or mesentery, which the veins descending into it weave, and through these most of the distribution takes place to the gates of the liver. The small intestine is joined to it, so that it seems to be part of it; for it resembles a jejunum stretched out. Next is the blind intestine (caecum), for receiving the nourishment. After this the colon, for receiving the residues separated out from the distribution; passing over to the right above the navel, inside the liver and the spleen, it is carried downward again, girdling the whole *epigastrion*, and ends at the rectum. There are, then, two passages beginning from the open space of the mouth. One is placed at the front of the neck and is called the windpipe, or rough artery. Where it begins, at the point where it opens, it is called the *pharynx*, or larynx. The whole passage is made up of cartilages like rings, or circles, so that it may remain uncollapsed, for the animal to breathe in without interruption; and for this reason its mouth is always open. For it is possible to endure abstaining from food for a very long time, but not breathing in, not even for an instant; and for this reason it keeps this passage clear for the pneuma, so that it may never obstruct the way for the pneuma. Indeed, if ever during eating something slips into it unnoticed, at once coughing and choking follow, until it is driven out by the pneuma and brought up. The rough artery sends the pneuma through into the lung and ends in the rough arteries within it, which are themselves also called *bronchia*. The gullet, lying further in than the windpipe, against the vertebrae of the neck, extends alongside the rough artery for a long way; but the windpipe, lying in front, running up while the food is being swallowed, is closed off exactly by the epiglottis, which grows from the root of the tongue. The epiglottis not only closes off the mouth [of the windpipe], but also ferries the food, licked up by the tongue as if by a winnowing-shovel, like a bridge, to the gullet, carrying it over the mouth of the windpipe. The gullet, having as its natural activity the appetitive faculty, is dilated by appetite and swallows what is brought in. And contracting on what lies within it, it as it were squeezes out and pushes these things toward the parts beneath, sending them through the diaphragm, being continuous with the mouth of the stomach, through which, being a narrow passage, the food passes into the belly. Of the belly, the natural activity digests the food brought to it. When digested, it first resembles barley-gruel. And through the so-called pylorus, which is narrower still, the food is filtered into the jejunum, which, being a thin intestine, was for this reason put together by nature into very many coils, so that it might not easily be cut through or torn apart. Its coils are held together and supported by the so-called *mesaraion*, or mesentery; and the *mesaraion* provides not only this service, but also [supports] the two veins growing out from the liver and then dividing into many branches, which run into the *mesaraion*, so that these too may not be torn, being slender. But they are held up by the support woven into it, making use of this and, lightened as by a gangway, they cross over, and so, [reaching] all the coils of the jejunum like leeches, opening into the jejunum, they receive all the food turned to juice in it. And as soon as they receive it they at once turn it into blood, it having been juice before, as long as it is in the jejunum. For the law of nature declares that no vessel is to contain blood, or phlegm, or anything else, from another source. Again, then, these veins received [it] through the *mesaraion*, and, having become two out of many, they run into the liver at its so-called gates. And as the food is turned into blood in the liver, each of the residues is separated out at the same time. The yellow bile is carried to the bladder in the liver, and the black to the spleen. From the liver the food, turned into blood, is distributed to the right ventricle of the heart. From the heart, through the jugular veins, the blood is distributed to the upper parts, and through the hollow vein (vena cava) to all the parts of the body. Then, as the watery part is separated from the blood from the hollow vein, branches carry [it] to the kidneys, which lie at the loins beneath the psoas muscles, through which the urine is filtered. It reaches the bladder through the so-called ureters. The bladder receives the urine in its body, and discharges it through the stalk (penis) to the outside. The testicles are glandular in consistency, and are receptacles and workshops of the seed, which is carried to them through the cremasters. Other vessels also descend into them which nourish them. They are enclosed by two coats, the one called reddish and the one called *dartos* (flayed). Over these is the scrotum. In women the womb resembles an inverted scrotum. Very many veins open into its interior, through which the blood is purged, which in conceptions is held back and goes to the nourishment and formation of the embryo; for two veins arising from the veins that weave the chorion, and two arteries from the arteries in it, and one nerve from the nerves, coming together, make up the *ourachos* (umbilical cord), which runs into the navel of the embryo, from which it grows and hangs. From the navel the veins give the blood to the gates of the liver in embryos; the arteries run into the thick artery (aorta) by the bladder; and this nerve [runs] into the spine.

[On osteology.] The joining of the bones is of two kinds: one for movement, and it is called a joint (*arthron*); the other for immobility, and it is called *synarthrosis*. Of this there are three kinds: suture, symphysis, gomphosis. By suture, then, the bones of the head are put together. Sutures are found in most [people] to be five: the coronal, through the *bregma* (forepart of the skull); the obelial, through the crown; the lambdoid, through the occiput; the temporal, two, one at each temple. The bones of the skull are seven: of the occiput one; of the crown two; of the temples two; of the forehead one; the multiform one. The brain has two outgrowths on either side of the cerebellum, which are called *korōnai*. They fit into the hollows of the first vertebra, in which, as on a pivot formed by the process of the second vertebra, the head turns to the sides, and tilts back and nods forward. After these, the so-called bony processes, two, a little apart, through which tendons and nerves pass down; then two others above the auditory passages, called the yoke-shaped (zygomatic) bones; under these two stone-like bones, these too. In front are the needle-shaped (styloid) outgrowths. They came into being for the distension of the *pharyngethron* (throat). And there is said to be a hyoid bone, at which their ends are bound together by cartilage. Above these are the nameless [bones], in front of which lies the multiform. By symphysis the bones of the upper jaw are put together. The face has nine symphyses: one placed at each of the eye-sockets; two at the sides of the nose and another in the middle cutting the nose in a straight line; two at the cheeks and two along the palate at the sides; and one dividing and cutting the palate in a straight line. Common to face and head are those at the zygomas. The bones of the face are twelve: of the nose two; of the eyes two; of the cheeks two; of the palate four; those of the tooth-sockets two, those resembling little wings. The lower jaw is, according to some, two bones grown together at the chin; according to some, one. By gomphosis the teeth are put together, for they are bolted into the sockets. They are thirty-two in number, in the upper and lower jaw: eight incisors, four canines, twenty molars. Of the other bones, the collarbones are bound by symphysis to the acromion, but to the breastbone they seem to make a mixture of joint and symphysis. They resemble in shape the Roman sigma (S), and that stretched out. Next are the ribs, twelve in all on each side. Seven of them join both the vertebrae of the spine and the breastbone on either side. The remaining five meet the spine at the back, but at the front, bending up toward one another, are bound together by cartilage. The vertebrae are twenty-four in all. They are divided: of the neck seven; of the back twelve; of the loins five. After all of them is the sacred bone (sacrum), which seems to be composed of vertebrae grown together with one another. The breastbone likewise also seems to be composed of seven bones grown together with one another in the sword-like shape. Each upper arm is fitted by a joint to the shoulder. It runs with its head obliquely into the hollow of the shoulder-blade. The shoulder-blades lie upon the muscles spread under the ribs from behind. The ulna and radius lie beside each other by symphysis, and they also meet the other head of the upper arm by a joint. For the upper arm fits with three of its condyles into the sigma-shaped notch of the ulna, and the radius turns about the fourth condyle as about a pivot. The bones of the wrist, being three, are bound to one another by symphysis, and are fitted by a joint to the ulna and radius. Those of the metacarpus are five; they too make a joint with those of the wrist, for they grow together with these. Those of the wrist are held together by symphysis with themselves and with those of the metacarpus, but meet the first phalanges of the fingers by a joint. The phalanges of the fingers are three to each, and their joining is by joint. Of the thigh there is one bone. It meets, with its moderately bent head, the deep socket of the hip, and is attached by a ligament growing out of the middle of the socket and growing into the middle of the head of the thigh-bone. The hip-bones, being two, lie by symphysis beside the sacred bone at the back, and beside each other at the front, where they are also called pubic bones. Of each shin there are two bones, that of the shin and that of the fibula. The fibula does not reach the knee joint, but only the end of the shin[-bone], which has in it four shallow impressions, into which it receives the condyles of the thigh, which are two. On them lies the kneecap, at the front, a round little bone, rather flat, like a small shield, holding their junction together, because they are jointed shallowly. The upper end of the fibula is grown together with the shin-bone below its epiphysis, and at the ankles the ends of the shin-bone and the fibula are bound to each other by a sinewy-cartilaginous ligament. It rests upon the talus, holding the bones within it. The talus, lying along the length of the foot, rests upon the fibula and is fitted to it immovably. With the bones of the shin and with the boat-shaped (navicular) bone at its front parts it meets by a joint. The boat-shaped bone, where it meets the talus, is hollowed, so that it seems boat-shaped. On the opposite side, being convex, it has three tracks, in which it receives the bronze-like bones, which are three. The cube-shaped (cuboid) bone has its position on the outside; it is jointed to the boat-shaped bone and the heel. It also has an outgrowth from below toward the front, under which the bone of the *tarsos* passes, to hold it up. Then the so-called *pedion*, itself also composed of five bones; then next are the five toes of the foot, all of three phalanges, composed like those of the hands, except the big one, for it alone was made of two. Their articulations are drawn together by certain membranous ligaments, but those at the talus and the heel by very strong ones, and some of these both round and sinewy-cartilaginous.

[On the humours, faculties and diseases, and their differences, causes and treatments.] The humours in the body, which are four from the first generation, are mixed with one another and blended through the body. But one abounds more in one place, another in another: blood in the heart, phlegm in the head, yellow bile in the liver, and black [bile] in the spleen. Of the innate pneuma there are two kinds: the natural and the psychic. Some also introduce a third, the cohesive (*hektikon*). Cohesive pneuma is that which holds stones together; natural, that which nourishes animals and plants; psychic, that which in ensouled beings makes animals capable of sensation and of moving with every motion. It is seated in animals, for animals are composed of the three. The psychic, then, dwells in the head, the natural in the heart, and the cohesive in the whole body. The natural activities, from the first generation, are conception and formation; and in those already born, appetite and swallowing, digestion in the stomach, distribution, conversion into blood, separation, nourishment, growth. There are separated in the body excrement, phlegm, biles, urine, sweats, mucus, saliva, milk. The psychic faculties are sensation and choice. The senses are five, which animals exercise through the organs of the body: sight, hearing, taste, smell and touch. The soul chooses some things without the body, reasoning or reflecting; with the body it chooses by moving it toward the taking in of certain things, or excretion, or motion from place to place. Breathing seems to be a compound activity, occurring in part by choice and in part without choice and naturally, as in sleep. A human being, then, is healthy when the first elements of which he is composed, and the second, the four humours from which he was formed, are in due proportion to one another in quantity and well harmonised in their qualities; when the solid bodies of which he is made up are neither divided, nor condensed, nor displaced from their own position; and when the pneumata are neither strained too much, as in the phrenitic, nor slackened, as in the lethargic, or in those in the cardiac condition, for in these the cohesive pneuma seems to be slackened. A human being is to be kept in health by using his accustomed exercises and the foods of the region observed in each season, guarding only against their excess, from which indigestions arise, from which diseases are formed. Diseases that are about to arise or will arise are to be forestalled. If from excess, one should employ abstinence from food, or purging, or phlebotomy; if from fatigue and deficiency, it is beneficial to rest and to nourish gently. All diseases arise, according to Hippocrates, some from outside, from the surrounding air, others from inside, from the regimen we take, by which one of the four humours either abounds, or falls short, or changes in quality. By these also the innate pneumata are some strained too much, others slackened to excess. And the solid bodies have many causes, both from within and from without, for suffering more affections. According to Erasistratus and Asclepiades, generally one cause [underlies] every disease: according to the one, the transfusion of blood into the arteries; according to the other, the distension of the corpuscles in the porous spaces. Signs of a disease-producing excess are swelling of the vessels, redness of the face, bulk of the whole body, and largeness of the pulses with vigour. When there is deficiency: collapse of bulk, thinness about the face, and small pulse with lack of tone. Fever, then, the ancients regard as an affection in itself; Erasistratus and some of the more recent [physicians], as a supervening effect. Fever is a turning of the innate heat toward the more burning, because it is turned back inward and hindered from breathing out. We recognise the feverish from heat that is intense and unremitting, and from the pulses: at the beginning of the onset of faint and irregular movement with frequency, at the peak of most vehement movement with elevation and excessive speed. According to the more recent, a heat brought up from the depth, greater than the natural, biting, sharp and persistent, together with frequency and hardness of the pulses, defines fever. The kinds of fevers according to all are two, the continuous and the intermittent. Continuous is that which does not cease into a fever-free interval before the disease is completely resolved. Again, of the intermittent there are six kinds according to the ancients: quotidian, tertian, quartan, quintan, septan, nonan. Quotidian is that which has an attack or remits every night or day; tertian, that with one [day] between; quartan, with two between; quintan, with three between; septan, with five between; nonan, with seven between. For the semitertian sometimes appears in continuous form, and is sometimes ranked among the intermittent. Of the other diseases there are two kinds, whether they be with fevers or without fever: some are acute, others chronic. The acute are these: phrenitis, *kausos* (burning fever), *synanche*, pleurisy, pneumonia, the cardiac condition, jaundice, cholera, ileus, the colic condition, apoplexy, tetanus, opisthotonus, emprosthotonus. The acute are generally formed by blood and yellow bile, abounding in certain parts of the body, in which they produce disease, turning toward the worse; the chronic likewise by phlegm and black bile, either multiplying much beyond the natural or changing toward the sharpest. Those ill from excess are to be treated by taking away, in regimen, from one ill from excess, whether through fasting, or purging, or phlebotomy; and by adding and giving to those who have fallen into disease from deficiency; and for those in whom indigestion and sharpness of the fluids is the cause, one must aid concoction with affusions and poultices, temper the sharp [fluids], and use well-juiced and moistening foods. The times for remedies, both in the disease as a whole and in its particular attacks, are four: beginning, increase, peak, decline. At the beginning of the whole disease abstinence from food is fitting until the third day. And in some cases the beginning of the whole [lasts] until the third day. Phlebotomy the more recent decide on at the beginning, until the third day; but the ancients employ it even after the third, if the strength holds up and the disease demands it. The time for food is after the three-day period according to the more recent; but according to the ancients not in all cases, but in those ill from excess, both young and older. In children they feed from the beginning, and in those with such a custom, whether because of the region or because of the climate. Before feeding, after the first three-day period, affusions of the head and of the middle parts are to be used; and in the following [days] poultices and clysters. The affusions, and always those on the middle parts, are to be employed warm and simple, boiling cumin or wood-dill [in them]; those on the head warm in lethargy and every drowsiness, but cooling in phrenitis and every acute fever. Of the poultices, some are prepared with honey and oil alone and are called softening; others with water-and-oil, which they name 'raw loosening'; others have things sprinkled on these, such as fine meal, linseed and fenugreek. Clysters [are made] with water-and-oil, honey, salt and a little natron. Their time is before food, in the remission of attacks and in the decline; in continuous [fevers], early morning. Phrenitis is a derangement of the mind with violent delirium, senseless moving about of the hands, plucking at the bedclothes, picking at straws, and acute fever. It arises for the most part from bile as cause. It is formed about the brain or the membranes, or, as some say, about the *phrenes*, which is called the diaphragm. The fitting treatment is this: if one foresees it at the beginning, depletion through phlebotomy and cupping, and a clyster and abstinence from food are fitting. Once the affection has set in, stupefying affusions, sleep-inducing ointments, and moistening foods. *Kausos* is a kind of fever, and is ranked by Hippocrates among the acute [diseases], as the quartan among the chronic, but by the more recent no longer. It is formed from bile, not very dry, about the small veins of the liver. It is treated by phlebotomy at the beginning and by giving cold water at the peak, or by cooling drinks, or by applications, such as that of boiled water-and-oil. *Kynanche* and *synanche* are inflammations about the neck: the one, *kynanche*, about its inside, choking acutely; *synanche* inclining more to the outside and therefore choking less and less dangerous. Each affection arises from bile or from salty phlegm. It is formed sometimes with acute fever, sometimes without fever. The most vigorous and quickest treatment is at once at the beginning by phlebotomy, and after this by phlegm-drawing drugs and cerates applied outside. Asclepiades even performs laryngotomy on those choking extremely. Pleurisy is an inflammation about the side, from within, with acute fever, violent pains and cough. It arises mostly from bile. The treatment at the beginning is phlebotomy; then that by poultices and dry fomentations, such as of millet and salt; third, that by drugs that cleanse from within, entitled pleuritic. In these, fluxes of the belly are to be guarded against. Pneumonia seems to some to be a heavy inflammation about the lung, and this is shown by the heaviness. To others it does not seem that the lung can be inflamed, but they say that the parts near it, coming into such a condition, cause it to be so named. This affection is formed with acute fever and by the same causes as pleurisy; according to some, by phlegm. The treatment is for the most part similar to that of pleurisy. The cardiac condition was not so named from the affection being about the heart, but because the ancients called the stomach *kardia*. When this is relaxed in an acute fever, the patients happen to be dissipated [by sweating]. The affection arises for the most part from immoderate fasting, or from untimely phlebotomy, or from some unreasonable depletion employed. So they need food that is easily distributed and warming, such as through wine and snow, and of solids those that are more nourishing and able to strengthen the stomach. But sometimes this also arises when the internal parts are inflamed, especially the liver; then, on the contrary, it needs depletion and the poulticing [used] for inflamed parts. Jaundice is an overflow of bile to the surface, sometimes with acute fever, sometimes also without fever, with burning of the internal parts and upset stomach. It needs, if the middle parts are inflamed, poultices first, and if excess underlies, phlebotomy; if not, things that empty the bile either through the belly and intestines, or through urine, or through the nostrils, or through sweats. Cholera is twofold according to Hippocrates: the one moist, which many know, with violent bilious excretion both below and above, and severe colic, with the convulsions and cramps that follow, especially in the calves. Care [consists] of warm affusions on the cramped parts, a bath after the purging, and food that is easily managed, easily distributed and good for the stomach. The other kind Hippocrates calls dry cholera, arising from the same cause and formed about the same parts, but without flux of the belly and vomiting. So it needs prior relaxation, also by poultices, and not giving [of food] but, on the contrary, deprivation. Ileus and the colic condition are inflammations of the intestines, the one of the small, the other of the colon. So the excrements are shut in, and the wind, rolling about in the intestines because it has no exit, causes violent pains and colic. Ileus is more acute both in its condition and its symptoms, and more dangerous. And vomiting of ileus-like [matter] occurs in those extremely ill with either affection. At the beginning ileus is best cured by phlebotomy, but mostly by fasting and by poultices that relax and resolve the inflammations. More effectively, colic drugs injected internally help, for they relieve the pains, bring on sleep and move the bowels. Apoplexy arises through an excess of thick fluids blocking the vessels from the head that distribute sensation and motion to the whole body; so the apoplectic become insensible, voiceless and motionless. Hippocrates says about this affection: 'A strong apoplexy is impossible to resolve, a weak one not easy.' Those seized should be phlebotomised at once, if their age agrees and their strength allows. Tetanus, opisthotonus and emprosthotonus are affections of the nerves. Each is a kind of spasm of the nerves from the head, through which it distributes motion to the body. It arises through blockage of the nerves by thick fluids: sometimes [of those] toward the back, so that one cannot bend forward, and it is called opisthotonus; sometimes of those toward the front, so that one cannot bend back, and it is called emprosthotonus; sometimes in a straight line, so that one cannot bend, and it has been named tetanus. It is treated by phlebotomy, if excess underlies, like the man in Hippocrates who fell and was wounded in the head. A copious affusion of cold water also cures them, especially in summer, if the sufferer is not thin but well-fleshed, for it brings about a recall of heat. But most use cerates that gently warm and relax, and similar ointments, and the application of oiled wool, and fomentations and warm poultices. The following chronic affections arise in the internal parts: headache, epilepsy, vertigo, dizzy spells with darkened vision, mania, melancholy, lethargy, coryza, hoarseness, catarrh, bringing up of blood, empyema in the thorax, consumption, abscess in the intercostal space, abscess at the collarbones, liver condition, tenesmus, dysentery, flat worms, round worms, threadworms, sciatica, arthritis, gout, elephantiasis; though this last is thought to belong to the external [affections]. Of the chronic [affections], then, headache is a settled pain of the head, sometimes recurring periodically, mostly set in motion [by something], arising from phlegm; sometimes the pain is in one part of the head, and it is called hemicrania. The cure of both is by removal of blood, or by a cupping glass on the occiput, and by drawing off phlegm, and by purging of the belly, and by applications, such as are recorded under the head of poultices, or emollient plasters, or salves; and finally the cause is dried up with a mustard plaster. Epilepsy, which they also call the sacred disease, arises at the origins of the nerves from the head, through which sensation and motion are distributed to the whole body. The cause of the affection, as Plato and Hippocrates say, is phlegm and black bile; that is why those held by the affection fall down, the paths of sensation and of motion being blocked in them; and they foam because of the agitation of the fluids, which comes from the spasm of the nerves; and that is why sometimes they also pass urine involuntarily. The affection is cured in children before puberty, when nature bursts forth around puberty and brings about a crisis of the disease, drying up the causes with the innate heat. For those past puberty the affliction is hard to cure, or even incurable. Dizzy spells and vertigo are akin to epilepsy, arising from the same causes and forming in the same regions. Their constitution, however, is superficial and not settled; therefore it is also more easily cured by purgings of the belly, especially with the sacred [remedy], then by drawings-off of phlegm and by vomitings employed in a cycle, some after dinner, others when fasting. And on top of all, it is set right with hellebore. Of derangement of the mind the two outstanding kinds are mania and melancholy; but there are many differences within these too, which have no names. Derangement of the mind, then, arises in the head as a whole. The cause of mania is yellow bile; for this reason those held by this affection are turbulent, unrestrained, and quick to violence. The cause of melancholy is black bile, a colder and gloomy humour; therefore such people are gloomy and despondent, suspicious of everything, misanthropic, and delighting in solitude, as Bellerophon is told of: 'He wandered alone over the Aleian plain, / eating out his heart, avoiding the paths of men.' The cure is by purgings of the belly, and especially that by vomiting; and on top of all, either hellebore is a resolution. Lethargy is an affection opposite to phrenitis: for it is a deep torpor, hard to rouse from, the sufferers forgetting everything they say; and these things accompany them in fever. The site of the affection is the head, for it arises around its membranes. Its cause is phlegm, a cold humour, which by its coldness and its moisture draws them down into sleep. The fitting treatment is the opposite of that for phrenitis: rubbing of the extremities with sharp and pricking substances, and the application of rousing things to smell; likewise foods that disperse and cut the phlegm, affusions of the head with drying substances, and in some cases poultices on the middle parts; for these, when inflamed, often press also on the origin of the nerves in the head.
