Coryza, hoarseness and catarrh: these affections begin from the head when it becomes filled and then drips down, sometimes into the nostrils, and it is called coryza, sometimes into the windpipe, and the affection is named hoarseness, sometimes into the thorax, and it is called catarrh. Coryza, then, is easy to cure and short-lived; hoarseness is second; for small meals and warm, grain-based foods have often delivered [people] from these affections. Catarrh is hard to cure and often incurable; for from a sharp and salty catarrh, as the bodies are eaten through, bringing up of blood occurs. The causes of bringing up of blood are three: either through erosion of the vessels, the blood flowing aside into the rough artery (trachea), it is brought up through the mouth; or through force, a rupture having occurred; or through weakness and lack of tone of the vessels, which do not hold tight but have opened their mouths, the blood leaking through. Discharge of blood and bringing up of blood differ. The one arises either from the lung or from the rough artery (trachea); the other from the gullet, and the blood appears darker, while that from the thorax is yellower and frothy; and further in that the one is brought up with a cough, the other without a cough. Often too blood carried down from the head through the openings of the palate into the mouth gives an appearance of bringing up which is not [real]. The places from which blood is properly brought up are three: first, the pharynx, and the bringing up of blood from here is less dangerous and easier to cure; second, from the rough artery (trachea), and this variety is hard to cure and dangerous; third, that from the lung, hardest of all to cure and most dangerous, upon which especially follow empyema and consumption, as Hippocrates says: 'Upon spitting of blood, spitting of pus; upon spitting of pus, consumption; upon consumption, death.' Some think that blood is also brought up from the side; but this mode is doubtful. The cure of bringing up of blood is for the blood to be checked, either by diverting it through phlebotomy, especially in the young, or by stopping it with vinegar-and-water, or by reducing the excess through abstinence from food, or through one of the simple drugs, such as acacia, hypocistis, balaustion, juice of plantain, and the like. Of empyema, the ancient cure is by cauteries that dry up the thorax and divert the flux to the outside; the more recent is to bring it to concoction with poultices and electuaries, then to clean it out quickly with drugs given by mouth, before the body is wasted. These drugs are inscribed specifically 'for those with empyema'. Empyemas that form in the intercostal spaces, when cut, have the discharge of the fluid specifically through a lint plug; for discharge all at once kills. Empyemas also form under the diaphragm, which they call abscesses 'in concealment'; they are not similarly dangerous or hard to cure; mostly they burst inward and are discharged that way, or when the outer tissues are divided. Diocles records that empyemas in the thorax too sometimes break into the artery leading to the kidneys and bladder, and are discharged that way with the urine. Consumption is properly so called when it is in the lung, or a wasting of the body [following] upon empyemas into the thorax. The affection is hard to cure, or even incurable. Milk-drinking at its very peak, drier places, Upper Egypt and Libya cure the affection best. A sciatic consumption is also spoken of by Hippocrates, the wasting of the body upon empyemas around the sacred bone (sacrum). Likewise also the nephritic [consumption]. Inflammations about the liver and spleen, if they change into empyema, these too waste the body moderately; but these empyemas are easier to cure and less dangerous than those in the lung. If they do not change, but the inflammations remain unconcocted and hardened, they bring bad conditions on the body, and in the end bring on dropsies. While they are simple inflammations, that about the liver brings on continuous fevers, that about the spleen for the most part quartans. For the cause of this type is black bile, whose vessel is the spleen; hence the remedy for a quartan is, before the shivering, to foment the extremities because of the coldness of the humour, and in the intervals the drawing off by vomiting. Of dropsies there are three kinds according to the more recent: ascites, tympanites, and the subcutaneous. According to Hippocrates there are two natures; for ascites and tympanites are of the same form. In both there is an outpouring of the nourishment, turned watery, into the space between the intestines and the peritoneum; but in ascites the water is more, the pneuma less, while in tympanites the pneuma is more, the fluid less. The subcutaneous [kind] is a dissolution of the solid bodies throughout the whole body into the nature of water. This Hippocrates too says is incurable. It is also called leucophlegmatia. The cause of every dropsy, as Erasistratus says, is inflammation of the liver or spleen that has become chronic and hardened. For by hindering the working-up of the nourishment in these viscera and its distribution to the whole body, it makes it watery, and once chilled it is poured out between the intestines and the peritoneum. According to Hippocrates, this too is incurable; but dropsy also arises without inflammation, especially the subcutaneous kind, when the innate heat is chilled and no longer masters the nourishment in the vessels; therefore the blood, chilled, turns watery and flows out through the veins, as oil will leak out of wineskins. For as long as it is blood in the veins, it is held exactly by the substance of the veins; but when the fattiness in it grows excessive, as with fat people, this, poured out, makes fat. Or the blood, turning watery or not being held tight, flows through, either into the space between the intestines and the peritoneum, or throughout the whole body. The cure of the two other dropsies is either by drying emollient plasters, or by diuretic drugs, or by laxative purgatives. Affected kidneys bring on violent pains, but in their case the affected place is hard to distinguish, because it is grown together with the outer tissues and the colon lies upon them; therefore when they come to suppuration they give an appearance of inflammation either in the outer parts or of a colic condition. And often the kidneys suffer in sympathy with the colon. The following affections arise about the kidneys: inflammation, ulceration, stone, paralysis. When there is inflammation, nothing is signalled through the urine, but rather it brings on pains which do not exactly reveal the primarily affected place, for the reasons we gave. The pains are hard to soothe, neither yielding to poultices nor giving way to removal [of blood] by cupping glass, but only, if at all, to certain nephritic drugs given internally. If there is ulceration, sometimes purulent matter is discharged through the urine, sometimes bloody matter. When there is stone, sometimes bloody matter is discharged, the tissues being roughened by the stone, sometimes gravel settles in the urine, if the stone is crumbly or is in the beginning of its formation. In paralysis the urine is passed bloody, as not being separated out. About the bladder these affections arise: paralysis, branny deposit, stone, ulceration, especially about the neck. Upon these supervene retention of urine, strangury, dysuria, both from these and from other causes. Inflammation is shown by pains about the pubic region and difficulty in passing urine. Inflammation of the bladder is resolved by a poultice, affusions, and scanty food; and if it is excessive, also removal of blood through phlebotomy. Ulceration is signified by bloody matter discharged at times, purulent at times, and sometimes mucous, and by pains about the pubic region. The cure is by applications, and especially by sweet-juiced and well-juiced food administered; also the things given internally for ulceration of the bladder, and the drug of Bissinus. Paralysis of the bladder is shown by the involuntary discharge of urine. The affection is hard to cure, or even incurable. A stone in the bladder is detected most precisely by the fingers let down into the rectum at the anus, so that the forefinger is bent at the tip toward the middle one and forward toward the bladder, where they meet the stone floating and bring it up into the neck of the bladder. The differences among stones are several: some of them are attached, others loose, and some easily broken, others hard to break. The attached ones, then, are for the most part hard to cure. Of the others, the easily broken ones drugs can dissolve and expel; the solid ones, hard to dissolve, the surgeons remove by cutting through the fleshy part of the bladder's neck. Retention of urine is the complete stoppage of urine; strangury is urination drop by drop; and dysuria produces only this, difficulty in urinating. These arise from many causes: sometimes from the stone wedged in the neck of the bladder and completely blocking the passage, or leaving something inside, or floating in the bladder. Retention of urine also arises from excessive inflammation of the bladder, and from immoderate filling, when the bladder cannot contract, and from sharpness of the urine, the neck being tightly contracted by the biting, and from a clot of blood shutting off the passage, and from thickness of urine that is held back. When the matter being discharged is concocted, such thickness should be drawn off; the clot should be dissolved with things able to melt it; and the filling emptied with the Erasistratean catheter. This resembles the Roman letter S. The beginning of the belly and intestines is the gullet, both in those in their natural state and in those in an unnatural condition. The affections of the gullet, then, are inflammation, ulceration, bringing up of blood, inflation, sogginess, loss of appetite, inability to retain what is taken. Inflammation is signified by a pain lodged there. Care is by affusions and poultices and grain-based, easily managed foods. Ulceration in the gullet is shown specifically by putrefaction, biting pain, and difficulty in swallowing. The cure is both by external applications and by well-juiced foods. Blood brought up from the gullet is checked by giving the things for bringing up of blood from the thorax, those written above. Inflation of the gullet is dispersed by the pore-opening [remedies] and whatever provokes belching. Sogginess is dried up by eating dry food and drinking wormwood. Loss of appetite arises in one case through phlegm lying beside [it], and one must dry up the cause; or through bile floating on the surface, and one must clean out the gullet; or [through the gullet] being unable to render its natural activity, the appetitive, just as eyes too become dim-sighted through lack of tone of the visual pneuma. For such loss of appetite one must give things that provoke and recall the appetite. The gullet becomes unable to retain what is taken both through sogginess and above all through lack of tone and weakness, just as a paralysed hand cannot hold whatever it touches. One must therefore tone and strengthen it, and then build up the whole body. Many of the affections of the gullet occur in the belly too, except loss of appetite. Failure to digest food is peculiar to the belly and occurs mostly in it, and the affection that follows this is diarrhoea. The other [affections] must be cured in the same way as those of the gullet. But diarrhoea must be examined carefully, to find for what cause it arises when the food has gone undigested. If it is through inflammation, apply poultices and affusions; if through phlegm lying beside [it] and producing sogginess, dry up the moisture by regimen; if from a quantity of bile, purge the bile; if through lack of tone, put tone into the body as for those lacking tone. If it is from the very quality of what has been taken, being hard to digest, or easily spoiled, or having something foreign in it, then after treating [the patient] one should forbid such things. Dysentery is an affection of the intestines. It arises after diarrhoea, when the corrupted matter lingers, eats through and ulcerates the intestines. It also arises from the start without diarrhoea, from some acrid humour that has eaten through the intestine. Sometimes dysentery also arises at the resolution of a disease, and Hippocrates forbids curing this, lest from its checking some other, greater disease supervene. That which has arisen from diarrhoea one cures with things that contract and stop the flux; that from some biting of an acrid humour one cures with things able to sweeten and temper it, washing out the ulcerated parts themselves by enema with similar things. When the affection is prolonged, however, [the patient] usually passes spreading and putrid matter, and then the injected pastilles are suitable, those compounded of realgar, lime, orpiment and the like. But when what is passed is not spreading, do not use these, since they bring on convulsion. And if such ulceration of the intestines is higher up, even so the pastilles must not be used, for they do not manage to reach the affected parts, and by fastening on the healthy ones they work destruction; instead use drugs [taken] from above, those recorded for dysentery. Lientery arises from dysentery, when, there being much ulceration in the intestines, many scars form, because of which the intestines do not master the food; hence it is called lientery, from the smoothness of the intestines. For this reason such lientery is also incurable, for scars cannot be cured. That which arises through lack of tone of the intestine is difficult and hard to cure. One should undertake treatment by putting tone into both the whole body and the intestines. Lientery also arises through phlegm washing over the intestines and making them slippery. And one must dry [it] up by fasting and by food that counters phlegm. Tenesmus arises specifically in the rectum. For when this is inflamed it produces continual straining and urges to evacuate, and this is tenesmus. The cure is by astringent fomentations from below, and grain-based, contracting food. If it persists, enemas of barley-gruel juice and goat suet must also be used. Worms are an affection of the intestines. There are three kinds of worms: the round, a span long or even longer, which also feed up as far as the gullet; the short, resembling longish grubs, which are called ascarides and form around the rectum; and the flat and elongated, so that they stretch along the whole intestine. These are also called 'girths' (keiriai), from resembling bed-girths, and likewise 'tapes' (tainiai). The round ones are easy to cure; they are abundant in children. The ascarides are more frequent in those past their prime, and are hard to cure and hard to expel, [yielding] only to acrid foods and to drugs compounded of bitter [aloes] and elecampane, mostly injected. Sciatica, arthritis and gout differ from one another only in magnitude; in their causes and in the places first affected they are the same. For they arise mostly from phlegm and form around the sinews that hold the joints together and give them movement. But sciatica arises around the joint at the hip, and often extends as far as the ankles. The cure is by bloodletting from the ankle, by cupping at the hip, by acrid clysters and by things that produce a kind of dysentery, and by external poultices, restoratives (akopa) and emollients. Gout forms only in the feet, and shows at its peak a feverish pain, so that it needs cooling things, and in its decline a numbing pain with chill, so that it needs warming things. Arthritis is the same affection as those just mentioned, forming in all the joints. It needs therapeutic drugs, warming cerates, and the appropriate regimen. Elephantiasis got the name of the affection from its likeness to the elephant. For the skin of those held by this affection is thicker and harder, bearing a resemblance to the skin of elephants. The cause of the affection is thick phlegm and black bile, or mucous [phlegm] above all, sown into [the body]. For these humours make it bestial. Hence the only effective therapy in those with elephantiasis is that by white and black hellebore. Some of the older [physicians] divide this affection into six: elephantiasis, leontiasis, ophiasis, lepra, alopecia and lōbē. They call elephantiasis the one resembling the elephant in skin and feet, for those who have fallen into this affection plainly have thick feet, just like those [animals]. They say those have leontiasis who have lumpy swellings, or oedematous ones, and are rather tawny like lions. Ophiasis is the one that strips the skin off those it seizes, as with snakes. Alopecia [is named] by transfer from those animals [foxes]. Lōbē is the one that destroys the extremities of hands and feet, and those deprived of such limbs [are called] 'mutilated'. Lepra is the one that roughens the skin and makes it look as it does on scaly things. Lichen too is itself an affection of the skin. There are two kinds of lichen: one mild and gentler, the other wild and more severe. In these, scales of the skin come away, and the place under the scales appears quite red and nearly ulcerated. The affection arises from salty phlegm and yellow bile; hence the scales come away from the skin as salt crusts do from earthenware jars. The cure is both by phlegm-drawing drugs and by external ointments. Lepra too is itself an affection of the skin, turning it whiter and rougher; the roughness is like that of raised pimples. Psora is more ulcerous. Each arises specifically from salty phlegm. The cure is by phlegm-drawing drugs and by external ointments, those recorded for lepra and psora. Alphos is a twofold affection, one white, the other black. The black arises from black bile; hence the melancholic [remedies] mostly relieve it. The white arises from phlegm, not salty. Leuke is an affection similar to white alphos, but it shows as a very white earth[-colour]. It differs from lepra in that the skin is smooth and not roughened, as in lepra. All these are relieved by phlegm-drawing drugs and external cleansing washes.

[On the best composition of a purgative.] Medication for internal [affections] is compounded of deobstruent, cutting, thinning, way-preparing, urging and purging [ingredients], and of correctives of the drugs' harmfulness, and of things good for the stomach and checking irrational flux. Deobstruents are whatever loosen the pores and make bodies free-flowing; cutting ones are whatever cut the humours and concoct them, thickening some and thinning others. Way-preparing ones are whatever lead and send the drugs ahead into the parts we wish: as, for those wishing to purge the liver, sandalwood; the spleen, hart's-tongue (skolopendrion); kidneys and hips, centaury and thlaspi; the back of the head, peony and stoechas; the front, marjoram and the like; chest, lung, thorax, heart, upper back and intestines, liquorice, storax and fenugreek seed; also almonds, saffron and mercury seed; and for the articulations and joints, each kind of hermodactyl; and other things for other parts, which must be inferred from what has been said. Urging ones are whatever move and urge on the drugs: as for agaric, iris; for Indian rhubarb, spikenard; for the pith of colocynth, tragacanth; for scammony, aloe, or cabbage juice, or [juice] of roses, or seeds. Likewise rock salt; for epithymum, as for euphorbium, bdellium and hellebore; radish seed and alypias; vinegar or chrysobalanos and myrobalans; bryony and elaterium, salt. And indeed also the root of pityusa, round hermodactyl, and similar things likewise for the others, which we went through in detail in the [work] On the Best Composition of Drugs, and what is lacking should be taken from there. Purging ones are those that purge, written of by us both here and in [the work] On Simple Drugs. Correctives of harmfulness are whatever have the property of opposing the noxious [qualities] of drugs: as ginger for agaric; for scammony juice, mastic or gum arabic, or camphor, [or] quince juice; for colocynth, almond oil; for alypias, mustard; as castoreum or hydromel for hellebore; and cinnamon for euphorbium; mastic for aloe, just as smyrnium urges it on; and the rest that we have mentioned in the [work] On the Best Composition. Things good for the stomach and checking the irrational flux of drugs are whatever tone, hold together and arouse the natural activities. To work these out in detail seemed superfluous to us now.

[On the division of therapy by drugs.] Pharmacy is twofold: one kind is for internal affections, and the dietetic physician uses it most; the other is for external ones, without which surgical work is not accomplished. Of pharmacy for internal [affections] there are twelve kinds: that for affections in the head; that of mouth remedies; that of digestives; that of cough remedies; that of pain-relievers; that of antidotes; that of purgatives. And there are specifically liver remedies, spleen remedies, kidney remedies, those for stones and ulcers in the bladder, and those for the womb. Among mouth remedies, some are for gums that bleed, rot or are eaten away, and for teeth, and others for aphthae and eschars, and for a relaxed uvula. Of the digestives, some are for weakness of the gullet or belly; some for inflation of these; some for bringing up of blood; some for pleuritic or peripneumonic patients; some for the consumptive; some for asthmatics or orthopnoeics; some for roughness of the artery and loss of voice. Of pain-relievers, some are for kidney patients, some for fluxes of the belly and dysenteries, and for colic and ileus patients; but in common all of them serve for every pain. Of antidotes, the simple ones are each for a different poison; but theriac is for all, both taken beforehand and given afterwards. Of purgatives, some purge from above, as those made with hellebore and all emetics; others are used from below, as those made with scammony, aloe, elaterium, colocynth, euphorbium, Cnidian berry and the like. Let those against broad worms be ranked third with these, such as the [preparation] made with stag's horn, mint and pepper. There is also a fourth kind, of those that purge the head alone through the mouth and nostrils, which are used specifically for affections in the head and eyes, and mostly for jaundice. Purgings through the upper parts suit the removal of chronic [diseases], and their right time is the intermissions. Those from below are suitable for acute diseases, pleurisies and peripneumonias; and the right time for all of them is the abatement of the individual paroxysms. Of pharmacy for external [affections] there are eleven kinds: some are dispersive, some maturative, some for fresh wounds, some pus-producing, some cleansing, some filling, some repressive, some cicatrizing, some for the eyes, some for the whole body, some caustic, for erysipelas, herpes and carbuncles; others are anointings, anti-fatigue and warming, effective for paralyses, arthritics, gout sufferers, all stiffening of the sinews, and tetanic and opisthotonic patients; others are detergents for what breaks out on the surface: leuke, alphos, lichen and lepra. The dispersive and maturative ones suit growths and every such abscess. Dispersive are all [plasters] made with salts and those made with natron, such as that of Ctesiphon. Maturative are those made with resin, galbanum and ammoniac incense. Of the drugs for fresh wounds, the grey ones suit recent wounds of the body; the specifically green and black ones, such as the *barbaros*, suit those in the head and dog bites. On ulcers, use pus-producing ones on inflamed ones, such as the four-drug [plaster]; cleansing ones on foul ones, such as the green [plaster] softened; filling ones on hollow ones; repressive ones on those with excess flesh, such as those made with *misy* and [copper] flakes, which also suit hard-to-stop haemorrhages. Caustics we use sometimes to divide and open bodies, as the covering of abscesses; sometimes on relaxed eyelids instead of stitching up, where by removing a proportionate amount [to form] a scar we draw up what is relaxed; sometimes we use them for intractable headache, diverting the fluxes outward by a deep eschar. The material of caustics is lye, unslaked lime, arsenic [orpiment], sandarach, burnt wine-lees and the like. Of head remedies, some suit achores, dandruff and eruptions, others headache and hemicrania. Of ear remedies, some are for inflammation of the ears, some for ulceration, some for ears running with pus, some for hardness of hearing, some for bruised ears. Of eye drugs there are seven kinds. Some suit beginning ophthalmias, as those made with *glaukion*, those with saffron, and the *kyknaria*; some are for [established] conditions, as the nard ones and those called *theodotia*; some for fluxes, as those made with frankincense, acacia and heath fruit; some for granulations, as those made with metallic substances, such as burnt copper, chalcitis and copper flakes. The fifth kind is that of collyria and dry sight-sharpening [powders] for xerophthalmia and psorophthalmia, which are of the same material as those described above. The sixth is the kind of liquids recorded for cataracts, which are prepared with galls, and especially that of the hyena. The seventh is the kind of poultices, used for extremely inflamed and very painful eyes; these are made with melilot, sweet wine, fenugreek and material of that kind. We smear around the eyelids at the start with repellents, such as those made with *glaukion* and those with saffron and *glaukion* alone; in settled [conditions] with drying and soothing ones, such as the nard ones and the *theodotia*. Those smeared on for beauty, such as those made with *sandyx* and *hedychroon*, belong not to medicine but to cosmetics.

[On the affections that arise in the eyes.] The following affections arise around the whole eye: disturbance, ophthalmia, *epiphora*, inflammation, oedema, emphysema, scirrhus, chemosis, carbuncle, squint, spasm, twitching, myopia, gangrene, putrefaction, ulcer, fistula, xerophthalmia, psorophthalmia, sclerophthalmia, prolapse, atrophy. Around the membranes these: rupture, erosion, distension, dilatation of openings, thickness, density, wrinkling, stretching, thinness. Around the inner side of the eyelids: roughness, thickness, *sykosis* (fig-growth), callosity, hardness, chalazion, sogginess, *mydesis* (rotting), fleshy growth, *poriasis* (callus). Around the outer side of the eyelids: hydatids, *lithiasis*, lice, *melikeris*, gangrene, growths, mutilations. Around the rim: *krithe* (stye), also [called] *posthia*, trichiasis, double rows, triple rows, *phalangosis*, burning, *ptilosis*, psoriasis, loss of lashes, paralysis. Common to the whole eyelids: paralysis, prolapse, eversion. Around the corners: *enkanthis*, *ankyle*, pterygium, *rhoias*, adhesion; outside, *aigilops*, *anchilops*. Around the white: pimple, ulcer, *hyposphagma* (bloodshot), abscess, chemosis, hollow ulcer, pterygium, *phakosis* (spot), jaundice, callus. Around the iris: *argemon*, *nephelion*, *achlys* (mist), burn, ulcer, *bothrion* (pit), blister, *myiokephalon*, staphyloma, *hypopyon*, rupture, scar, leucoma, hollow ulcer, protrusion, *onyx*, suppuration, ulceration. Around the pupil: cataract, glaucoma, mydriasis, wasting, *synchysis*, dilatation of the pupil, amaurosis, wrinkling, night-blindness, day-blindness, myopia, suppuration. Around the passages: rupture, transfusion, collapse, ulceration, carbuncle formation. Disturbance, then, is when the eye, having been stirred up superficially and moderately, becomes quite reddish. Ophthalmia is when the white is red and the eyelids raised, with closing of the lids being painful and touching with the hands sore. Inflammation is an intensification of the redness and of the swelling of the lids, so that one looks up with pain. *Epiphora* is a common name throughout the whole body, both for violent inflammation coming on and for copious fluxes flowing in; but specifically it is said of the eyes, when a mass of flux flows in with very great inflammation. Oedema is when [the eye] appears swollen and paler, or even hard to move; sometimes the white also rises above the black. Emphysema is when the eye suddenly swells and becomes paler and more phlegmy; it occurs for the most part in old people, especially in summer. Scirrhus arises through intensification of chronic inflammation, the flesh growing and becoming livid. The eye is said to suffer flux not only when it is red but also when it discharges much tear. Xerophthalmia is when the corners are ulcerous, rather rough and itchy, the lids are red, and a salty, natron-like tear trickles out. Sclerophthalmia is when the lids are rather hard and the eye itself is hard to move and red. Prolapse is when the eye, being movable, falls forward with inflammation. They speak of atrophy of the eye when, from a long illness or from some unclear cause, it is first as if pushed out a little, then becomes hollow, aching at its roots, grows smaller, and sees dimly or not at all. The lids are called rough when, turned out, they appear rather bloody, rougher, fleshier and like millet seeds. Thick lids are those which, turned out, appear harder than normal and fleshier than rough ones. *Sykosis* is when the inside of the lids grows flesh resembling flesh with a protrusion, and the whole eye is hard to move. Callosity is when the granulations in the lids through age are thicker, whiter and insensitive, and therefore become hard to rub away. *Skleriasis* is a swelling with redness on the lid and pain, hard to rub away and more chronic than inflammation. Chalazion is certain round, well-defined swellings on the inside of the lid, resembling hail. Sogginess is soft bodies, old indeed and very pale, on the inside of the lids, not yet having roughness; hence it is called sogginess. *Mydesis* is a common name for [parts] of the body perishing from putrefaction; the same thing happens also around the lids, and they appear more bulky and continually suffer flux, more fat forming about them. *Krithe*, which is also called *posthia*, is when on the inside of the lids by the rims an elongated suppuration forms, like a barleycorn in shape; other larger ones also occur in the middle of the lids, called *krithe*. *Lithiasis* is when, the lids being turned out, there are things like calluses around the lids, white and thick and like stones, pricking the eye. We say the lids are lousy when many small flat lice appear about the hairy parts. The eye is said to have double lashes when, beneath the natural hairs, others grow up underneath, prick the eye and cause flux. *Ptilosis* is when others grow underneath while the natural ones fall in and break, causing pricking. *Phalangosis* is when there is a double or triple row of hairs growing underneath on the upper or lower lid. The eye is said to be paralysed when its natural movements fail it and it cannot look up or look down, and is insensitive; this often happens also to certain parts of the eye. They say the lids are everted when they are turned out further after ulceration in ophthalmias. They speak of *enkanthis* when from ulceration the corner by the nose grows excess flesh; seafarers suffer this most. They speak of pterygium when, the white having been ulcerated further and grown excess flesh, a thin sinewy membrane runs over the eye, beginning from one of the corners, until it touches the black and the top. *Rhoias* occurs in the eye when, from some unclear cause, the corner wastes away, or is removed by surgery, and is no longer able to hold in the tear, but [the eye] suffers flux. The lids grow onto either the white or the black from ulceration; if they grow onto the black, they prevent sight completely, if onto the white, less so; it is called *ankylosis*. They speak of *aigilops* or *anchilops* when an abscess forms by the corner next to the nose containing pus, or, breaking, greases the bone, or pours out its fluid either into the corner or into the nose. *Psydrakion* is a term used generally of the whole body, and it occurs also on the white of the eye, like an eruption red at its tip. An ulcer occurs on the black or the white when the outer skin is divided, crescent-shaped or round in form, rather hollow, of the same colour or whitish. They speak of *hyposphagma* when, the vessels in the first coat having burst from a blow, blood passes underneath between the fibrous layer of the white and the inner coat, and at first the colour of the eye is bloody, later livid. Chemosis is when from rather violent inflammation both lids turn out and do not cover the whole eye. But properly chemosis is said when the white on either side of the iris is inflamed, becoming hollow at the iris, similar in shape to the [shellfish] called *cheme*. Hollow ulcers are the name in the eye for round, hollow ulcers, broader than *bothria*, that form in it around the iris. *Argemon* is when along the circle of the iris and the white, and sometimes also the black, a round and whitish ulcer forms. *Nephelion* is a superficial ulcer, a little larger than *argemon*, and white. *Achlys* is over the whole of the black, from superficial ulceration: a very thin scar like misty air. *Epikauma* is when the outer skin, burnt on the surface, ulcerates, or also becomes slightly deeper, arising from great epiphora. *Bothrion* is a hollow ulcer, clean, narrow, like round pricks, deeper than an *helkydrion*. They speak of *phlyktaina* [blister] when, from ulceration or even without ulceration, on the surface of the horny coat a very thin membrane, lifted up, takes fluid in beneath it, or else when a thicker fluid runs in under the fibrous layer of the coat and produces the blister. *Myokephalon* is when, the first coat having been eaten through by ulceration, the second coat protrudes at the iris so as to resemble a fly's head. *Staphyloma* is said when the pupil of the eye is raised up with inflammation and pain and becomes like a grape, white in colour. *Hypopyon* is when pus surrounds the whole iris, or half of it. *Rhexis* [rupture] is an ulceration from a blow or some other cause, carrying down in depth, for the most part, the division of all the membranes, so that even the fluids with which we see pour out. A scar is when on the black of the eye, from an ulcer that was deep, a thickening of the membrane forms and the colour appears whiter. It also forms on the so-called white membrane, but does not show. *Leukoma* is the same as the so-called scar, but differs in that from ulceration a large scar, greater and thicker, forms on the iris, which they call *leukoma*. *Helos* [nail] is a solid prominence of the black, with a smooth and white, as it were fleshy, scar; often it also rises on the white where it joins the black. Some say there is a cataract when it happens that an infusion of some fluid occurs at the pupil, often with congealing, so as to prevent sight, or else to dim it in appearing. *Glaukosis* is a change of the crystalline fluid to a white and watery colour, through which sight is prevented. *Mydriasis* is said when the pupil is in no way altered in colour, but is much broader than is natural, so as to approach the circle of the iris and impede sight. Consumption is said when the pupil narrows, so as to resemble a prick, and becomes dimmer and more wrinkled, either from dangerous illnesses or from intense headaches. *Synchysis* is when the fluids in the eye do not stay in place, keeping their proper order, but are disturbed. *Amaurosis* is when there is a total impediment of sight, without evident cause. They speak of *nyktalopes* when they see more dimly by day, but more brightly when the sun sets, and still more at night; or the opposite, a little by day, but in the evening or at night not at all. They call *myopes* those who see things close by but do not see things far off. *Diapyesis* is a collection of a smaller amount of fluid around the pupil itself, hard to evaporate and hard to disperse, drier than a cataract. Rupture of the channel occurs about the eye when the channel stretching from the brain and membrane to the eye is torn off, so that complete blindness results, a blow about the head having preceded, or a fall from a height, from which the rupture of the channel occurs. *Paremptosis* is when fluid falls into the channel, through the opening or rupture of a vessel, and blocks the channel from the very base of the brain, from which the eye too has its power of sight, so that sight is impeded, with pains. *Symptosis* [collapse] occurs from the channel narrowing and collapsing through atrophy and paralysis. This affection is rare and hard to cure. *Anthrakosis* is a scabbed ulcer with spreading and flux, and sometimes a swollen gland and fevers, occurring over all the rest of the body, and sometimes also about the eyes.

[On the affections of the outside of the head.] About the outside of the head the following form, which have not been recorded among the chronic [affections], concerning the fractures of the skull in the head. Of these there are five differences: fissure, *engeisoma*, *ekpiesma*, *apechema*, vaulting; [also] separation of sutures, hydrocephalus, *achores*, scurf, *melikeris*, *atheroma*, *kerion*. About the hairy part of the head and the chin: alopecia, ophiasis, *madarotes* [loss of eyelashes], baldness. In all, hairs fall out, become thin, break, split, become dry, become downy, become yellowish, turn grey. The affections about the eyes have been recorded separately. Those about the ears: bruising, *pterygomata*, fracture of the cartilage, excess or lack of earwax, hardness of hearing, deafness, flow of pus, foul-smelling flux. About the nose the following form: ozaena, polyp, ulcer, fracture, distortion, crushing, flattening. About the mouth: rotting of the gums, decay of the teeth, toothache, falling out of the sockets, abscess on the tongue, *epoulis*, *paroulis*, aphthae, scabbing; *paristhmia* [swollen tonsils], *staphyle* [swollen uvula], *sykoma*. About the face: freckle, *ionthoi* [pimples], *phakos* [mole]. Fracture of bones. Separation of the junctions. Dislocations of the lower jaw from the upper. About the neck: synanche, kynanche, strangling, displacement of vertebrae, scrofulous swellings, steatomas. About the shoulders: fracture of the acromion, separation. About the elbow: *melikeris*, *atheroma*, steatoma, watery fluid. About the wrists: ganglia. About the fingers and toes: chilblains, paronychia. Local [affections] wherever in the body they happen to be: inflammation, swelling, *emphysema*, hardening, abscess, clean ulcer, dirty ulcer, hollow ulcer, overfleshy, scabbed, dry ulcer, fluxing, burrowing, callused, fistulous; putrefaction, *phyma*, boil, *therminthes*, *phygethlon*, *chalaza*, *phagedaina*, blisters, carbuncles, *epinyktides*, erysipelas, herpes. About the breasts specifically, and about the private parts of woman and man, carcinomas. There also forms, wherever in the body it may be, hidden carcinoma, ulcerated carcinoma, *therioma*. About the groin: simple buboes, suppurating growths. About the knees: knee pains, fluxes, calluses. About the back of the knee: steatomas, *ankyle* [contracture]. About the shin: varicose veins. In the calf: hardening, Chironian ulcers. About the extremities of the foot: blackenings, mortifications, gout, fistulas. About the heels: scales.

[On the affections of the skin.] About the skin and places over the whole body: *lepra*, *psora*, white alphos, black alphos, leuke, simple lichen, wild lichen, *drakontiasis*, *akrochordones* [pedunculated warts], *thymoi*, *myrmekiai*, corns, calluses, some from gout and arthritis, others also on their own. About the seat: blind haemorrhoids, fissures, prolapse, condylomas, *pylides*. There also occurs prolapse of the whole womb to the outside. About the scrotum: enterocele, cirsocele, epiplocele, sarcocele, porocele, steatocele. About the bones in the whole body: caries, *sphakelos*, fracture without wound or with wound, *ekbyrsosis*. There are five differences of fractures: splinter-like, stalk-like, radish-like, nut-like, meal-like. Bones become black sometimes in fractures, sometimes without them. About all the joints: displacements, slight shifts, dislocations, subluxations, *syndesis*, callus formation, fluxes, separation of junctions.

[On the kinds of surgery.] Surgery is the methodical removal of what is properly called foreign, by incisions and settings together with the treatment of wounds and ulcers, applied to the human body. Surgery has two general operations, joining and dividing. Of these there are many kinds. Kinds of joining are: setting of broken bones, bandaging, reduction of dislocated [joints], replacing of prolapsed intestines, womb and rectum, suture of the belly, and drawing together of mutilations, as of noses, lips and ears. Kinds of dividing are: simple incision and excision, *hypospathismos*, *periskythismos*, *angeiologia*, cutting out, cautery, scraping, filing, sawing out. Simple incision, then, we use for all abscesses. One should divide along the length of the limb and not crosswise. Excision for those in the armpits, groin, buttocks and seat, excising in a myrtle-leaf shape. *Hypospathismos* at the forehead for fluxing eyes, and *periskythismos* for those of the crown and for a prepuce that has turned black. Cutting out for limbs that are turning black and for fractures in the head. For all [affections] about the bones cautery, scraping, filing and sawing are useful, and in many others. Cautery with cauteries we use particularly for all [lesions] already spreading, and for fluxing eyes, hips, or even internal [parts]. For cauteries are employed also for consumptives, for those with spleen trouble, for arms prone to dislocate into the armpit, for aigilops, for [parts] turning black or being sawn, because of vessels that open, and for those otherwise haemorrhaging. These then are the [affections] that form about the head of those subject to surgery. Of fractures about the head there are five kinds: fissure, *engeisoma*, *ekpiesma*, *apochema*, vaulting; and according to some six, [adding] *trichiasis*, that is, the superficial scoring of the bones. Of hydrocephalus there are four kinds: one between brain and membrane, one between membrane and bone, one between bone and pericranium, one between bone and skin. About the skin there form *melikeris*, *atheroma*, and on the outside alopecia. Alopecias we scarify; *melikerides* and *atheromas* we remove with the fluids in them, dividing the surface in a myrtle-leaf shape or simply, then peeling off the coats with the fingers. Hydrocephali under the skin and pericranium we empty with some two or three straight incisions; those under the bones by cutting out; those between membrane and brain are incurable. Every kind of fracture in the head is subject to cutting out, by means of chisels removing the broken part of the bones. The ancients cut them out by sawing with crown-saws turned by a rotating [strap]; those after them with trepans, making seats for the chisels; those of today are content with chisels alone. Of affections about the eyes these are subject to surgery: trichiasis, *hydatides*, *enkanthides*, pterygia, staphylomas, cataracts, chronic and excessive fluxes, stones in the eyelids, adhesion [of the lids] to the [eye], [and] of those about the eyes aigilops. Slackened eyelids we stitch up and down, removing from them a strip of suitable size and following the shape of the lids; in those not slackened, by looping up the hairs with a needle. The *hydatides* we remove [by] setting [them] apart. *Enkanthides*, pterygia and staphylomas we excise, staphylomas by passing a thread through and tying them off, pterygia and *enkanthides* by drawing them up either with a thread or with a hook. Cataracts we couch, puncturing near the iris from the part toward the small corner until [the needle] enters empty space; then, turning it slantwise toward the iris, with its tip we bring down the fluid collected at the pupil, scraping and pressing, so that it does not rise again. Flux is stopped by *hypospathismos*, *periskythismos* and *angeiologia*. *Hypospathismos* is done by making three incisions above the forehead, then passing the spatula-probe through the tissues between. *Periskythismos* is as follows: the forehead is divided by transverse incisions, like a crown; and on the other part of it, a little above the temples, certain triangles are removed, resembling in shape the letter Δ. *Angeiologia* is performed by dividing the hidden vessels deeply from temple to temple. Stones in the eyelids we cure by dividing the lid widely and removing the stone without disturbance. Adhered eyelids we open out and separate with a scalpel [and] plucking razors; aigilops we excise down to the bone and burn through with cauteries. Some, instead of the cautery, pierce the bone with a trepan, as far as the nose. Of what forms in the nose, polyps we excise with a narrow small scalpel and afterwards scrape away the roots with a scraper. Ozaenas are for the most part incurable; the same operation [is used] for these too. Of those in the mouth, *epoulides* and *paroulides* we divide once we have brought them to suppuration. Immoderately slackened uvulas we cut out, grasping them with forceps; teeth we extract, scoring around them. Glands in the tonsil region swollen beyond nature we excise with tonsil-knives. Steatomas and scrofulous swellings in the neck we remove by dividing the surface, peeling with the fingers, and loosening the network of vessels. Ganglia occur for the most part in the metacarpus, and mostly in women who work wool; we crush them, and they also subside when softened with cerates. Growths and scrofulous swellings in the armpits we cut with excision, and likewise those in the groin. Abscesses between the ribs we divide, but make the discharge of pus not all at once, but in measure. Some also burn them through. Carcinomas occur in many parts of the body, but especially about the breasts. They are excised wherever they are and burnt through with cauteries not very fiercely heated. Some cut and burn through at once with heated razors. All those who have the navel protruding are called *exomphaloi*. They have three differences: some are *pneumatomphaloi*, some *enteromphaloi*, some *hydromphaloi*. All the differences are subject to surgery, a double thread being passed through with a needle and the navel tied round. Dropsical patients we puncture a little below the navel, from the left, with an iron myrtle-leaf [lancet], until it enters empty space. For those lacking foreskin the surgery is twofold: some are undercut from the inside, others divided superficially in a circle from outside, so that the prepuce may be drawn forward. Those with phimosis of the foreskin are operated on by drawing back the foreskin as far as possible, then freeing the calluses that appear with a phlebotome superficially. *Hypospadiai* are those who from birth have the urethra underneath, below the so-called frenum. They are to be treated by perforating the tip of the glans and inserting a small tube. The so-called imperforate, whether they have a thin opening or none at all, are operated on thus: letting down the point of the phlebotome we open further, then, putting the finger beneath, we free all round. Those with a stone in the bladder we cut, wedging the stone in the neck of the bladder, and using a stone-chisel we divide at one stroke the overlying tissues and remove the stone with a stone-forceps. Those with *rhyas*, however they have arisen, we restore by cutting away the callus if it is very large. Those troubled by retention of urine because of its quantity, the bladder being stretched and unable to contract, we relieve by drawing off the urine through a catheter. The catheter resembles the Roman sigma, S. It is let down into the penis through the urethra as far as the bladder, we having in it a thread which holds at its tip a little wool projecting slightly; this is first soaked in the urine and then drawn outwards, and the urine follows it, as though it were guiding it towards discharge. Of the swellings that form about the scrotum there are seven kinds: hydrocele, porocele, steatocele, sarcocele, epiplocele, cirsocele, enterocele. There are also cases in which these are combined, such as hydrenterocele and sarcoepiplocele. In hydroceles, then, one must divide the scrotum and, meeting at its most veined part the tunic that contains the fluid, empty it and further remove the excess of the tunic. In cases where there is no tunic, we are content to let out the fluid. Steatoceles and poroceles must be cut, likewise laying the left hand over the scrotum, then dividing superficially until we reach the fat, or the callus, or whatever it may be, and we remove this. Sarcocele patients are also operated on in the same way. One must cut away only the whitish flesh that presents itself, and the red flesh, by skinning it off and separating it, and then remove what remains. In cirsoceles, stretching [the skin] up with a hook, divide superficially, take up the varix and skin it, leaving about the breadth of a little finger, and stretching up the rest, cut it off. Take careful guard where the cremasters or the testicles are entangled [with it]. Enterocele and epiplocele patients we cut thus: pressing back the intestine or the omentum carefully, we then remove the spermatic duct as far as we can. If not, drawing the peritoneum forward and noosing it, we cut it away. Haemorrhoids we tie off by passing a fine double thread through their bases, and after two hours we cut them off. Of fistulas some are non-perforating, having only a mouth; others are perforating, either inwards into the anus or outwards. In those perforating into the anus, pass the probe through, then, inserting the finger into the seat, draw the gut out with the tip of the probe and cut round, beginning from below. Likewise also with those outside the seat. In the non-perforating, pierce through all the healthy tissue with the sharp end of the probe. Some, instead of slitting open or cutting away the tissue between the perforations, [pass] a twisted linen thread on the tip of the probe, and, holding the divided parts, tie off the intervening tissue with it, tightening the threads each day; they cut through what lies between, and, removing the callus, heal it over with the Egyptian [ointment]. This method was first recorded by Hippocrates. Varicose veins in the legs we first mark from outside with scratched lines along their whole length; then, laying [the patient] down and taking up the skin superficially, we divide it first; then, drawing the varix up with a hook, we tie it off, and having done this at all the incisions, we either extract it with a varix-extractor, cutting through the ends, or, catching it with a double-ended probe with thread through the hollow of the varix, we draw it out by turning it back. The so-called *drakontia* [guinea worms] are similar to varicose veins; they cause great pain when they move, protruding a little. One must therefore divide, as with varicose veins, skin [them] off and so extract them. Corns, calluses, *akrochordones*, *thymoi* and *myrmekiai* we cut out and cauterize, or sprinkle with the *psorikon* [itch powder]. Mutilations about the nostrils, ears or lips are restored to their natural state thus: the lips we make bleed by paring them all round with a small scalpel, then bringing them together we stitch them rather closely. Towards the cheeks, from either end of the lips, where they have grown together, we divide inside and outside and hold them apart with lint, so that the flesh in growing does not produce slackness. Mutilations of the ears or nostrils, when the cartilage has been divided, must be excised of cartilage and so stitched with a woollen thread.

[On fractured limbs and dislocated parts.] Fractured limbs are set by extension and grow callus by bandaging. Of fractures about the head, in how many ways they occur and how they are treated, has been said. And if a fracture occurs in the face, treat it like those in the head, chiselling out the affected bone. One must also know which fractured bones are untreatable. If the nose is fractured, it is not straightened. Hippocrates says the ear too is fractured, because the cartilage imitates bone and seems hard to restore to its former shape. But if the nose sinks in at its middle from the palate, as he says, it becomes snub, untreatable. If the clavicle is fractured, or the collarbone, or any rib, these too are for the most part hard to restore. On the collarbones especially one must apply [pads] and bandage from armpit to armpit. If any of the larger limbs is fractured, or of the smaller parts, such as the phalanges of the fingers, or the bones of the wrist, or of the metacarpus, or of the tarsus, all break in large pieces, stalk-like, radish-like, or splinter-like, and in small pieces nut-like or meal-like. First, then, in all fractures one must, while bandaging and extending very strongly and firmly, separate [the fragments] and draw them well apart from each other, so that they may be set and restored to their former shape. The bones must be set not all straight, but to the shape of the paired limb: if it is straight, in a straight line; if curved or otherwise bent, likewise. The method of preparing bandaging for all is to make a bandage of old linen cloths, suited to the breadth and size of the limb: in breadth, for the largest, four or five fingers; for the slenderer, not less than three fingers. The rule of bandaging is this. The first bandage proceeds from the fracture upwards for three turns, for the most part. The second begins from the same place, the turns being reversed: it proceeds downwards and is brought back upwards, so as to be double the first. It is to be soaked in water-and-oil, or wine-and-oil, or sweet oil, until the first three-day period, then in a dissolved, liquid cerate, so as to be like thick oil. It must not press very hard, so that [the limb] does not mortify, but so as to lie on and be firmly fitted, nor yet loosely, so that it holds together and repels what flows in, so as not to become inflamed. Then, making three- or four-fold pads, apply them, filling out the thickness of the limb, so that they neither overlap one another nor leave gaps by standing apart. Over these, putting on a third bandage, proceed from the fracture downwards, go up to the upper parts and end there. The first unbandagings are every third day; those after the seventh at longer intervals, according to pressing needs. Splints, made of real fennel-stalk, [are applied] over the last bandage, wool being placed underneath, the splints arranged at intervals, when [the limb] is quite free of inflammation, the convex parts of the stalk taken off on the outside and the smooth side applied on the inside with a small knot, and tied on them either with little strips or with sailor's cord. In fractures with a wound, instead of all these, [they] make two- or three-fold pads, each filling the thickness around the limb so that its ends are separate yet overlap each other, and keeping the whole limb laid in these as needed. First they apply [them] to the body soaked in the aforementioned [liquids]; over these they keep wool laid beforehand, and bands simply over the wool, along the seat placed beneath of the open trough. This method of bandaging is especially suitable for meal-like fractures, with wounds and much bruising of the muscles, in which also tents must be placed beforehand soaked in suitable [liquids]. Of tents there are five kinds: twisted, scraped, plucked, wick-shaped, *priapiskos*-shaped. In dislocations extension must likewise come first; and the reduction proper to each is employed after the extension. All are set on the Hippocratic bench, being extended and fitted together at the same time. The head dislocates, for it is articulated with the first vertebra of the neck towards the second. The lower jaw is displaced from the zygoma at the cheekbones, and it is reduced with the hands alone, being brought from this side and that to where it fits against the upper [jaw]. When the shoulder slips into the armpit only, the reduction is by the *ambe* with extension. There are also others, called wrestlers' [methods]. Of dislocations of the elbow there are four differences: one inwards, one outwards, one forwards, one backwards. Those outwards or inwards we reduce thus, with extension, bringing the displaced bones back the opposite way; those backwards or forwards without extension: for the one is reduced by sudden flexion, something being placed in the bend of the elbow, the other by rather forceful extension. Dislocations of the wrist, metacarpus and fingers are set by slight extension of the hands. Every distortion of the spine, hunchback, inward curvature and scoliosis, cannot be corrected. The head of the femur at the hips falls either inwards towards the peritoneum, or outwards to the opposite side, and backwards into the buttock and forwards into the groin. The four differences are incurable. At the knee, dislocation outwards is frequent and the restoration easy by flexion. Inwards it both occurs and is restored less often. Still more rarely backwards. Forwards it does not occur at all, for the bones are never displaced, because of the kneecap holding them together, unless this too is fractured. At the ankles a slight displacement, when it occurs, is hard to restore; a great and violent one does not even admit correction, for it is very dangerous, also if it occurs with a wound. Toes, when dislocated, are straightened like those of the hands. All separations of the junctions themselves, as in the face and of the ulna and radius, of the tibia and fibula, of the metacarpus and tarsus, are also restored to their former state. Parts that blacken and spread [with gangrene], whether from fractures or violent constriction, we often saw off, whole limbs. Likewise also those already seized by [the poison of] venomous creatures. Then with cauteries heated very hot we stop the spreading. After the cauteries we apply a poultice of green leek with salt, then, when the scabs have come away, we treat [them] as ulcers. Bites of venomous creatures we do not want to heal over quickly, but we take pains that the ulcers flux as much as possible.
